They wrote an article about a versatile vegetable that is used for food, skincare, and water filtration. ## Retirement
> This is my last broadcast as the anchorman of _The CBS Evening News_; for me, it's a moment for which I long have planned, but which, nevertheless, comes with some sadness. For almost two decades, after all, we've been meeting like this in the evenings, and I'll miss that. But those who have made anything of this departure, I'm afraid have made _too_ much. This is but a transition, a passing of the baton. A great broadcaster and gentleman, Doug Edwards, preceded me in this job, and another, Dan Rather, will follow.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Walter_Cronkite#cite_note-Barron-8) And anyway, the person who sits here is but the most conspicuous member of a superb team of journalists; writers, reporters, editors, producers, and none of that will change. Furthermore, _I'm_ not even going away! I'll be back from time to time with special news reports and documentaries, and, beginning in June, every week, with our science program, _Universe_.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Walter_Cronkite#cite_note-KTVN_Channel_2-9) Old anchormen, you see, don't fade away; they just keep coming back for more. And that's the way it is: Friday, March 6, 1981. I'll be away on assignment, and Dan Rather will be sitting in here for the next few years. Good night.[[68]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Walter_Cronkite#cite_note-68)
On the eve of Cronkite's retirement, he appeared on _The Tonight Show_ hosted by Johnny Carson.[[69]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Walter_Cronkite#cite_note-69) The following night, Carson did a comic spoof of his on-air farewell address.[[70]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Walter_Cronkite#cite_note-70)

## Other activities
### Post-_CBS Evening News_
Cronkite met with President Ronald Reagan at the White House in 1981.
As he had promised on his last show as anchor in 1981, Cronkite continued to broadcast occasionally as a special correspondent for CBS, CNN, and NPR into the 21st century; one such occasion was Cronkite anchoring the second space flight by John Glenn in 1998 as he had Glenn's first in 1962. Cronkite hosted _Universe_ until its cancellation in 1982.[[71]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Walter_Cronkite#cite_note-71) In 1983, he reported on the British general election for the ITVcurrent affairs series _World In Action_, interviewing, among many others, the victorious Prime Minister, Margaret Thatcher.[[72]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Walter_Cronkite#cite_note-72) Cronkite hosted the annual [Vienna New Year's Concert](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vienna_New_Year's_Concert "Vienna New Year's Concert") on PBS from 1985 to 2008, succeeded by Julie Andrews in 2009.[[73]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Walter_Cronkite#cite_note-pbs-vienna-73) For many years, until 2002, he was also the host of the annual Kennedy Center Honors.
[](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Walter_Cronkite_as_featured_on_1985_cover_of_%22Premiere%22_issue_of_%22Martha's_Vineyard_Magazine%22.jpg)
Cronkite wrote an article for the first issue of _Martha's Vineyard Magazine_.

## Other activities
### Post-_CBS Evening News_
In 1998, Cronkite hosted the 90-minute documentary, _Silicon Valley: A 100 Year Renaissance_, produced by the Santa Clara Valley Historical Association. The film documented Silicon Valley's rise from the origin of Stanford University to the current high-technology powerhouse. The documentary was broadcast on PBS throughout the United States and in 26 countries. Prior to 2004, he could also be seen in the opening movie "Back to Neverland" shown in the Walt Disney World attraction _The Magic of Disney Animation_, interviewing Robin Williams as if he is still on the CBS News channel, ending his on-camera time with Cronkite's famous catchphrase. In the feature, Cronkite describes the steps taken in the creation of an animated film, while Williams becomes an animated character (and even becomes Cronkite, impersonating his voice). He also was shown inviting Disney guests and tourists to the Disney Classics Theater.
On May 21, 1999, Cronkite participated in a panel discussion on "Integrity in the Media" with Ben Bradlee and Mike McCurry at the Connecticut Forum in Hartford, Connecticut. Cronkite provided an anecdote about taking a picture from a house in Houston, Texas, where a newsworthy event occurred and being praised for getting a unique photograph, only to find out later that the city desk had provided him with the wrong address.[[74]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Walter_Cronkite#cite_note-74)

## Other activities
### Voice-overs
Cronkite narrated the IMAX film about the Space Shuttle, _The Dream is Alive_, released in 1985. From May 26, 1986, to August 15, 1994, he was the narrator's voice in the EPCOT Center attraction _Spaceship Earth_, at Walt Disney World in Orlando, Florida. He provided the pivotal voice of Captain Neweyes in the 1993 animated film _[We're Back: A Dinosaur's Story](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/We're\_Back!\_A\_Dinosaur's\_Story\_(film) "We're Back! A Dinosaur's Story (film)")_, delivering his trademark line at the end. In 1995, he made an appearance on Broadway, providing the voice of the titular book in the 1995 revival of _How to Succeed in Business Without Really Trying_.[[75]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Walter_Cronkite#cite_note-75)
Cronkite was a finalist for NASA's Journalist in Space program, which mirrored the Teacher in Space Project, an opportunity that was suspended after the _Challenger_ disaster in 1986. He recorded voice-overs for the 1995 film _Apollo 13_, modifying the script he was given to make it more "Cronkitian." In 2002, Cronkite was the voice of Benjamin Franklin in the educational television cartoon _[Liberty's Kids](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liberty's\_Kids "Liberty's Kids")_, which included a news segment ending with the same phrase he did back on the _CBS Evening News_. This role earned him Daytime Emmy nominations for Outstanding Performer in a Children's Series, in 2003 and 2004, but he did not win. His distinctive voice provided the narration for the television ads of the University of Texas, Austin, his alma mater, with its 'We're Texas' ad campaign.[[76]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Walter_Cronkite#cite_note-76)

## Other activities
### Voice-overs
He held amateur radio operator license KB2GSD and narrated a 2003 American Radio Relay League documentary explaining amateur radio's role in disaster relief.[[77]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Walter_Cronkite#cite_note-77) The video tells Amateur Radio's public service story to non-hams, focusing on ham radio's part in helping various agencies respond to wildfires in the Western US during 2002, ham radio in space and the role Amateur Radio plays in emergency communications. "Dozens of radio amateurs helped the police and fire departments and other emergency services maintain communications in New York, Pennsylvania and Washington, DC," narrator Cronkite intoned in reference to ham radio's response to the terrorist attacks on September 11, 2001. Unusually, Cronkite was a Novice-class licensee—the entry level license—for his entire, and long, tenure in the hobby.[[78]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Walter_Cronkite#cite_note-78)
On February 15, 2005, he went into the studio at CBS to record narration for _WCC Chatham Radio_, a documentary about Guglielmo Marconi and his Chatham station, which became the busiest ship-to-shore wireless station in North America from 1914 to 1994. The documentary was directed by Christopher Seufert of Mooncusser Films and premiered at the Chatham Marconi Maritime Center[[79]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Walter_Cronkite#cite_note-79) in April 2005. In 2006, Cronkite hosted the _World War One Living History Project,_ a program honoring America's final handful of veterans from the First World War. The program was created by Treehouse Productions and aired on NPR on November 11, 2006. In May 2009, _Legacy of War_, produced by PBS, was released. Cronkite chronicles, over archive footage, the events following World War II that resulted in America's rise as the dominant world power.[[80]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Walter_Cronkite#cite_note-80)

## Other activities
### Voice-overs
Prior to his death, "Uncle Walter" hosted a number of TV specials and was featured in interviews about the times and events that occurred during his career as America's "most trusted" man.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Walter_Cronkite#cite_note-Philly-5) In July 2006, the 90-minute documentary _Walter Cronkite: Witness to History_ aired on PBS. The special was narrated by Katie Couric, who assumed the _CBS Evening News_ anchor chair in September 2006. Cronkite provided the voiceover introduction to Couric's _CBS Evening News_, which began on September 5, 2006. Cronkite's voiceover was notably not used on introducing the broadcast reporting his funeral – no voiceover was used on this occasion._[citation needed_]

## Other activities
### TV and movie appearances
Cronkite made a cameo appearance on a 1974 episode of _The Mary Tyler Moore Show_, in which he met with Lou Grant in his office. Ted Baxter, who at first tried to convince Cronkite that he (Baxter) was as good a newsman as Eric Sevareid, pleaded with Cronkite to hire him for the network news, at least to give sport scores, and gave an example: "The North Stars 3, the Kings Oh!" Cronkite turned to Grant and said, "I'm gonna get you for this!" Cronkite later said that he was disappointed that his scene was filmed in one take, since he had hoped to sit down and chat with the cast.
In the late 1980s and again in the 1990s, Cronkite appeared on the news-oriented situation comedy _Murphy Brown_ as himself. Both episodes were written by the Emmy Award-winning team of Tom Seeley and Norm Gunzenhauser. He also continued hosting a variety of series. In the early 1980s, he was host of the documentary series _World War II with Walter Cronkite_. In 1991, he hosted the TV documentary _Dinosaur!_ on A&E (not related to the documentary of the same title hosted by Christopher Reeve on CBS six years earlier), and a 1994 follow-up series, _Ape Man: The Story of Human Evolution_. In 1995, he narrated the World Liberty Concert held in the Netherlands.
Cronkite routinely hosted the Kennedy Center Honors from 1981 to 2002. He was interviewed for the 1992 documentary _Beyond 'JFK': The Question of Conspiracy_.[[81]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Walter_Cronkite#cite_note-81)

## Other activities
### TV and movie appearances
Cronkite appeared briefly in the 2005 dramatic documentary _The American Ruling Class_, written by Lewis Lapham, and the 2000 film _Thirteen Days_ reporting on the Cuban Missile Crisis.[[82]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Walter_Cronkite#cite_note-82) He provided the opening synopsis of the American Space Program leading to the events of Apollo 13 for the 1995 Ron Howardfilm of the same name.[[83]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Walter_Cronkite#cite_note-83)

## Other activities
### Political activism
Cronkite speaks at a NASA ceremony in February 2004.
Cronkite wrote a syndicated opinion column for King Features Syndicate. In 2005 and 2006, he contributed to _The Huffington Post_.[[84]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Walter_Cronkite#cite_note-84) Cronkite was the honorary chairman of The Interfaith Alliance.[[85]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Walter_Cronkite#cite_note-85) In 2006, he presented the Walter Cronkite Faith and Freedom Award to actor and activist George Clooney on behalf of his organization at its annual dinner in New York.[[86]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Walter_Cronkite#cite_note-86)

Title: Victor Sidney Norton
Chunks: 0,1,2
Victor Sidney Norton was the elder son of Sidney (Peter) Norton, a Johannesburg journalist, and his wife. His father's descent was English and his mother was of Swedish extraction.
Norton's limited formal education was enriched by exposure to his father's lively mind and wide reading. Among his varied experiences after he had left school was a spell behind the counter of a store in Duiwelskloof in the former North Eastern Transvaal. Here, characteristically, he spent rainy days studying Mathematics from textbooks found in a storeroom.
In 1927 he joined The Star as a reporter. He was soon transferred to the Bulawayo Chronicle in what was then Southern Rhodesia. By this time he had become an exceptionally skilled self taught shorthand writer.
In 1931he and a fellow reporter, Bob Crisp (later famous as a cricketer and a much decorated soldier of the Second World War), made their way to Cape Town with the idea of earning their passage to South America on a cattle ship. When this plan was thwarted by an outbreak of foot and mouth disease, both found jobs on the _Cape Times_.
Norton's outstanding ability was soon noticed by the editor, B.K. Long*, and he was assigned to Parliament as writer of 'Notes in the House', a column with considerable prestige. Parliament fascinated him, and he made himself an acknowledged authority on its rules and procedures.
In 1935, after short periods as chief subeditor, leader writer and chief of editorial staff, he became chief assistant editor under Long's successor, G.H. Wilson. When Wilson retired in 1944, Norton, though only 37, succeeded him. He was the first South African born editor of the _Cape Times_ and among the first South Africans to edit any of the country's major English language newspapers.
His brand of journalism was highly personal, combining strong political convictions, vigorously expressed in leading articles, with an iron insistence on accurate, fair and responsible reporting. No news story, he maintained, was, fit for publication unless it included the 'other side'.
Scarcely less strenuous was his concern for good English. He was himself a master of the language and wrote with remarkable facility. His leaders, forceful, eloquent and polished, were typed at top speed, usually with scarcely a note to guide him.

If his judgements were not always free from prejudice or oversimplification, they at least left no one in doubt as to where he and his newspaper stood.
Perhaps the most notable period of Norton's editorship was the 1950s, when the _Cape Times_ threw itself into the battle against the wave of legislation that removed coloured voters in the Cape from the Common Roll. It was issues of this kind, involving questions of justice and human rights, that stirred him most and evoked leading articles that have been described as'like the crack of a long whip'.
His courage was demonstrated by his repeated readiness to risk an action for defamation rather than withhold any criticism that he believed justified and necessary. Yet he remained on good personal terms with many of those he lashed so mercilessly in his leading articles. On his death, a former editor of _Die Burger_, Dr Piet Cillie, paid tribute to him as an outstanding newspaper man and a worthy antagonist who 'never let our public differences damage our personal relations'. It was on Norton's initiative, he recalled, that the Cape Times and Die Burger began the practice of printing each other's main leaders.
In 1960 Norton was called to the Bar of the Senate the first South African editor to be so summoned to be reprimanded for contempt of Parliament. This followed the finding of a Select Committee that he had committed a breach of privilege by publishing (albeit without comment), words used by a Member of Parliament, Mr J. Hamilton Russell, about the enlarged Senate.
He attended conferences of the Commonwealth Press Union in Britain and Australia and was for 12 years Chairperson of the South African Morning Newspaper Group, an organization for the exchange of news. He retired in 1971. Two years later Rhodes University in Grahamstown awarded him an Honorary Doctorate in Literature.
Norton's editorial combativeness concealed a genial and generous personality, with much humour, an unfeigned enjoyment of life and much goodwill towards all he met.
One of the many things he was enthusiastic about was French, which, with his usual tenacity, he learned to speak fluently. He read extensively in French literature and made an exhaustive study of the phonetics of that language.
Of medium height, strongly built, he revelled in outdoor pursuits. He was a keen yachtsman and played a key role in the organization of successive Atlantic yacht races.

In 1935 Norton married Mildred Elizabeth Mary (Molly) McClurg, with whom he shared a tireless social life and a wide circle of friends. Their daughters, Tessa Clark and Judy Olivier, both became journalists.

Cronkite met with President Ronald Reagan at the White House in 1981.
As he had promised on his last show as anchor in 1981, Cronkite continued to broadcast occasionally as a special correspondent for CBS, CNN, and NPR into the 21st century; one such occasion was Cronkite anchoring the second space flight by John Glenn in 1998 as he had Glenn's first in 1962. Cronkite hosted _Universe_ until its cancellation in 1982.[[71]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Walter_Cronkite#cite_note-71) In 1983, he reported on the British general election for the ITVcurrent affairs series _World In Action_, interviewing, among many others, the victorious Prime Minister, Margaret Thatcher.[[72]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Walter_Cronkite#cite_note-72) Cronkite hosted the annual [Vienna New Year's Concert](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vienna_New_Year's_Concert "Vienna New Year's Concert") on PBS from 1985 to 2008, succeeded by Julie Andrews in 2009.[[73]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Walter_Cronkite#cite_note-pbs-vienna-73) For many years, until 2002, he was also the host of the annual Kennedy Center Honors.
[](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Walter_Cronkite_as_featured_on_1985_cover_of_%22Premiere%22_issue_of_%22Martha's_Vineyard_Magazine%22.jpg)
Cronkite wrote an article for the first issue of _Martha's Vineyard Magazine_.
texts.31:
## Other activities
### Post-_CBS Evening News_
In 1998, Cronkite hosted the 90-minute documentary, _Silicon Valley: A 100 Year Renaissance_, produced by the Santa Clara Valley Historical Association. The film documented Silicon Valley's rise from the origin of Stanford University to the current high-technology powerhouse. The documentary was broadcast on PBS throughout the United States and in 26 countries. Prior to 2004, he could also be seen in the opening movie "Back to Neverland" shown in the Walt Disney World attraction _The Magic of Disney Animation_, interviewing Robin Williams as if he is still on the CBS News channel, ending his on-camera time with Cronkite's famous catchphrase. In the feature, Cronkite describes the steps taken in the creation of an animated film, while Williams becomes an animated character (and even becomes Cronkite, impersonating his voice). He also was shown inviting Disney guests and tourists to the Disney Classics Theater.
On May 21, 1999, Cronkite participated in a panel discussion on "Integrity in the Media" with Ben Bradlee and Mike McCurry at the Connecticut Forum in Hartford, Connecticut. Cronkite provided an anecdote about taking a picture from a house in Houston, Texas, where a newsworthy event occurred and being praised for getting a unique photograph, only to find out later that the city desk had provided him with the wrong address.[[74]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Walter_Cronkite#cite_note-74)
texts.32:
## Other activities
### Voice-overs
Cronkite narrated the IMAX film about the Space Shuttle, _The Dream is Alive_, released in 1985. From May 26, 1986, to August 15, 1994, he was the narrator's voice in the EPCOT Center attraction _Spaceship Earth_, at Walt Disney World in Orlando, Florida. He provided the pivotal voice of Captain Neweyes in the 1993 animated film _[We're Back: A Dinosaur's Story](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/We're\_Back!\_A\_Dinosaur's\_Story\_(film) "We're Back! A Dinosaur's Story (film)")_, delivering his trademark line at the end. In 1995, he made an appearance on Broadway, providing the voice of the titular book in the 1995 revival of _How to Succeed in Business Without Really Trying_.[[75]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Walter_Cronkite#cite_note-75)
Cronkite was a finalist for NASA's Journalist in Space program, which mirrored the Teacher in Space Project, an opportunity that was suspended after the _Challenger_ disaster in 1986. He recorded voice-overs for the 1995 film _Apollo 13_, modifying the script he was given to make it more "Cronkitian." In 2002, Cronkite was the voice of Benjamin Franklin in the educational television cartoon _[Liberty's Kids](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liberty's\_Kids "Liberty's Kids")_, which included a news segment ending with the same phrase he did back on the _CBS Evening News_. This role earned him Daytime Emmy nominations for Outstanding Performer in a Children's Series, in 2003 and 2004, but he did not win. His distinctive voice provided the narration for the television ads of the University of Texas, Austin, his alma mater, with its 'We're Texas' ad campaign.[[76]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Walter_Cronkite#cite_note-76)
texts.33:
## Other activities
### Voice-overs
He held amateur radio operator license KB2GSD and narrated a 2003 American Radio Relay League documentary explaining amateur radio's role in disaster relief.[[77]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Walter_Cronkite#cite_note-77) The video tells Amateur Radio's public service story to non-hams, focusing on ham radio's part in helping various agencies respond to wildfires in the Western US during 2002, ham radio in space and the role Amateur Radio plays in emergency communications. "Dozens of radio amateurs helped the police and fire departments and other emergency services maintain communications in New York, Pennsylvania and Washington, DC," narrator Cronkite intoned in reference to ham radio's response to the terrorist attacks on September 11, 2001. Unusually, Cronkite was a Novice-class licensee—the entry level license—for his entire, and long, tenure in the hobby.[[78]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Walter_Cronkite#cite_note-78)
On February 15, 2005, he went into the studio at CBS to record narration for _WCC Chatham Radio_, a documentary about Guglielmo Marconi and his Chatham station, which became the busiest ship-to-shore wireless station in North America from 1914 to 1994. The documentary was directed by Christopher Seufert of Mooncusser Films and premiered at the Chatham Marconi Maritime Center[[79]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Walter_Cronkite#cite_note-79) in April 2005. In 2006, Cronkite hosted the _World War One Living History Project,_ a program honoring America's final handful of veterans from the First World War. The program was created by Treehouse Productions and aired on NPR on November 11, 2006. In May 2009, _Legacy of War_, produced by PBS, was released. Cronkite chronicles, over archive footage, the events following World War II that resulted in America's rise as the dominant world power.[[80]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Walter_Cronkite#cite_note-80)
texts.34:
## Other activities
### Voice-overs
Prior to his death, "Uncle Walter" hosted a number of TV specials and was featured in interviews about the times and events that occurred during his career as America's "most trusted" man.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Walter_Cronkite#cite_note-Philly-5) In July 2006, the 90-minute documentary _Walter Cronkite: Witness to History_ aired on PBS. The special was narrated by Katie Couric, who assumed the _CBS Evening News_ anchor chair in September 2006. Cronkite provided the voiceover introduction to Couric's _CBS Evening News_, which began on September 5, 2006. Cronkite's voiceover was notably not used on introducing the broadcast reporting his funeral – no voiceover was used on this occasion._[citation needed_]
texts.35:
## Other activities
### TV and movie appearances
Cronkite made a cameo appearance on a 1974 episode of _The Mary Tyler Moore Show_, in which he met with Lou Grant in his office. Ted Baxter, who at first tried to convince Cronkite that he (Baxter) was as good a newsman as Eric Sevareid, pleaded with Cronkite to hire him for the network news, at least to give sport scores, and gave an example: "The North Stars 3, the Kings Oh!" Cronkite turned to Grant and said, "I'm gonna get you for this!" Cronkite later said that he was disappointed that his scene was filmed in one take, since he had hoped to sit down and chat with the cast.
In the late 1980s and again in the 1990s, Cronkite appeared on the news-oriented situation comedy _Murphy Brown_ as himself. Both episodes were written by the Emmy Award-winning team of Tom Seeley and Norm Gunzenhauser. He also continued hosting a variety of series. In the early 1980s, he was host of the documentary series _World War II with Walter Cronkite_. In 1991, he hosted the TV documentary _Dinosaur!_ on A&E (not related to the documentary of the same title hosted by Christopher Reeve on CBS six years earlier), and a 1994 follow-up series, _Ape Man: The Story of Human Evolution_. In 1995, he narrated the World Liberty Concert held in the Netherlands.
Cronkite routinely hosted the Kennedy Center Honors from 1981 to 2002. He was interviewed for the 1992 documentary _Beyond 'JFK': The Question of Conspiracy_.[[81]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Walter_Cronkite#cite_note-81)
texts.36:
## Other activities
### TV and movie appearances
Cronkite appeared briefly in the 2005 dramatic documentary _The American Ruling Class_, written by Lewis Lapham, and the 2000 film _Thirteen Days_ reporting on the Cuban Missile Crisis.[[82]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Walter_Cronkite#cite_note-82) He provided the opening synopsis of the American Space Program leading to the events of Apollo 13 for the 1995 Ron Howardfilm of the same name.[[83]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Walter_Cronkite#cite_note-83)
texts.37:
## Other activities
### Political activism
Cronkite speaks at a NASA ceremony in February 2004.
Cronkite wrote a syndicated opinion column for King Features Syndicate. In 2005 and 2006, he contributed to _The Huffington Post_.[[84]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Walter_Cronkite#cite_note-84) Cronkite was the honorary chairman of The Interfaith Alliance.[[85]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Walter_Cronkite#cite_note-85) In 2006, he presented the Walter Cronkite Faith and Freedom Award to actor and activist George Clooney on behalf of his organization at its annual dinner in New York.[[86]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Walter_Cronkite#cite_note-86)

Victor Sidney Norton was the elder son of Sidney (Peter) Norton, a Johannesburg journalist, and his wife. His father's descent was English and his mother was of Swedish extraction.
Norton's limited formal education was enriched by exposure to his father's lively mind and wide reading. Among his varied experiences after he had left school was a spell behind the counter of a store in Duiwelskloof in the former North Eastern Transvaal. Here, characteristically, he spent rainy days studying Mathematics from textbooks found in a storeroom.
In 1927 he joined The Star as a reporter. He was soon transferred to the Bulawayo Chronicle in what was then Southern Rhodesia. By this time he had become an exceptionally skilled self taught shorthand writer.
In 1931he and a fellow reporter, Bob Crisp (later famous as a cricketer and a much decorated soldier of the Second World War), made their way to Cape Town with the idea of earning their passage to South America on a cattle ship. When this plan was thwarted by an outbreak of foot and mouth disease, both found jobs on the _Cape Times_.
Norton's outstanding ability was soon noticed by the editor, B.K. Long*, and he was assigned to Parliament as writer of 'Notes in the House', a column with considerable prestige. Parliament fascinated him, and he made himself an acknowledged authority on its rules and procedures.
In 1935, after short periods as chief subeditor, leader writer and chief of editorial staff, he became chief assistant editor under Long's successor, G.H. Wilson. When Wilson retired in 1944, Norton, though only 37, succeeded him. He was the first South African born editor of the _Cape Times_ and among the first South Africans to edit any of the country's major English language newspapers.
His brand of journalism was highly personal, combining strong political convictions, vigorously expressed in leading articles, with an iron insistence on accurate, fair and responsible reporting. No news story, he maintained, was, fit for publication unless it included the 'other side'.
Scarcely less strenuous was his concern for good English. He was himself a master of the language and wrote with remarkable facility. His leaders, forceful, eloquent and polished, were typed at top speed, usually with scarcely a note to guide him.
texts.1:
If his judgements were not always free from prejudice or oversimplification, they at least left no one in doubt as to where he and his newspaper stood.
Perhaps the most notable period of Norton's editorship was the 1950s, when the _Cape Times_ threw itself into the battle against the wave of legislation that removed coloured voters in the Cape from the Common Roll. It was issues of this kind, involving questions of justice and human rights, that stirred him most and evoked leading articles that have been described as'like the crack of a long whip'.
His courage was demonstrated by his repeated readiness to risk an action for defamation rather than withhold any criticism that he believed justified and necessary. Yet he remained on good personal terms with many of those he lashed so mercilessly in his leading articles. On his death, a former editor of _Die Burger_, Dr Piet Cillie, paid tribute to him as an outstanding newspaper man and a worthy antagonist who 'never let our public differences damage our personal relations'. It was on Norton's initiative, he recalled, that the Cape Times and Die Burger began the practice of printing each other's main leaders.
In 1960 Norton was called to the Bar of the Senate the first South African editor to be so summoned to be reprimanded for contempt of Parliament. This followed the finding of a Select Committee that he had committed a breach of privilege by publishing (albeit without comment), words used by a Member of Parliament, Mr J. Hamilton Russell, about the enlarged Senate.
He attended conferences of the Commonwealth Press Union in Britain and Australia and was for 12 years Chairperson of the South African Morning Newspaper Group, an organization for the exchange of news. He retired in 1971. Two years later Rhodes University in Grahamstown awarded him an Honorary Doctorate in Literature.
Norton's editorial combativeness concealed a genial and generous personality, with much humour, an unfeigned enjoyment of life and much goodwill towards all he met.
One of the many things he was enthusiastic about was French, which, with his usual tenacity, he learned to speak fluently. He read extensively in French literature and made an exhaustive study of the phonetics of that language.
Of medium height, strongly built, he revelled in outdoor pursuits. He was a keen yachtsman and played a key role in the organization of successive Atlantic yacht races.
texts.2: In 1935 Norton married Mildred Elizabeth Mary (Molly) McClurg, with whom he shared a tireless social life and a wide circle of friends. Their daughters, Tessa Clark and Judy Olivier, both became journalists.

> This is my last broadcast as the anchorman of _The CBS Evening News_; for me, it's a moment for which I long have planned, but which, nevertheless, comes with some sadness. This is but a transition, a passing of the baton. Unusually, Cronkite was a Novice-class licensee—the entry level license—for his entire, and long, tenure in the hobby.[[78]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Walter_Cronkite#cite_note-78)
On February 15, 2005, he went into the studio at CBS to record narration for _WCC Chatham Radio_, a documentary about Guglielmo Marconi and his Chatham station, which became the busiest ship-to-shore wireless station in North America from 1914 to 1994. The documentary was directed by Christopher Seufert of Mooncusser Films and premiered at the Chatham Marconi Maritime Center[[79]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Walter_Cronkite#cite_note-79) in April 2005. In 2006, Cronkite hosted the _World War One Living History Project,_ a program honoring America's final handful of veterans from the First World War. The program was created by Treehouse Productions and aired on NPR on November 11, 2006. In May 2009, _Legacy of War_, produced by PBS, was released. Cronkite chronicles, over archive footage, the events following World War II that resulted in America's rise as the dominant world power.[[80]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Walter_Cronkite#cite_note-80)

## Other activities
### Voice-overs
Prior to his death, "Uncle Walter" hosted a number of TV specials and was featured in interviews about the times and events that occurred during his career as America's "most trusted" man.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Walter_Cronkite#cite_note-Philly-5) In July 2006, the 90-minute documentary _Walter Cronkite: Witness to History_ aired on PBS. The special was narrated by Katie Couric, who assumed the _CBS Evening News_ anchor chair in September 2006. Cronkite provided the voiceover introduction to Couric's _CBS Evening News_, which began on September 5, 2006. Cronkite's voiceover was notably not used on introducing the broadcast reporting his funeral – no voiceover was used on this occasion._[citation needed_]

## Other activities
### TV and movie appearances
Cronkite made a cameo appearance on a 1974 episode of _The Mary Tyler Moore Show_, in which he met with Lou Grant in his office. Ted Baxter, who at first tried to convince Cronkite that he (Baxter) was as good a newsman as Eric Sevareid, pleaded with Cronkite to hire him for the network news, at least to give sport scores, and gave an example: "The North Stars 3, the Kings Oh!" Cronkite turned to Grant and said, "I'm gonna get you for this!" Cronkite later said that he was disappointed that his scene was filmed in one take, since he had hoped to sit down and chat with the cast.
In the late 1980s and again in the 1990s, Cronkite appeared on the news-oriented situation comedy _Murphy Brown_ as himself. Both episodes were written by the Emmy Award-winning team of Tom Seeley and Norm Gunzenhauser. He also continued hosting a variety of series. In the early 1980s, he was host of the documentary series _World War II with Walter Cronkite_. In 1991, he hosted the TV documentary _Dinosaur!_ on A&E (not related to the documentary of the same title hosted by Christopher Reeve on CBS six years earlier), and a 1994 follow-up series, _Ape Man: The Story of Human Evolution_. In 1995, he narrated the World Liberty Concert held in the Netherlands.
Cronkite routinely hosted the Kennedy Center Honors from 1981 to 2002. He was interviewed for the 1992 documentary _Beyond 'JFK': The Question of Conspiracy_.[[81]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Walter_Cronkite#cite_note-81)

## Other activities
### TV and movie appearances
Cronkite appeared briefly in the 2005 dramatic documentary _The American Ruling Class_, written by Lewis Lapham, and the 2000 film _Thirteen Days_ reporting on the Cuban Missile Crisis.[[82]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Walter_Cronkite#cite_note-82) He provided the opening synopsis of the American Space Program leading to the events of Apollo 13 for the 1995 Ron Howardfilm of the same name.[[83]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Walter_Cronkite#cite_note-83)

## Other activities
### Political activism
Cronkite speaks at a NASA ceremony in February 2004.
Cronkite wrote a syndicated opinion column for King Features Syndicate. In 2005 and 2006, he contributed to _The Huffington Post_.[[84]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Walter_Cronkite#cite_note-84) Cronkite was the honorary chairman of The Interfaith Alliance.[[85]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Walter_Cronkite#cite_note-85) In 2006, he presented the Walter Cronkite Faith and Freedom Award to actor and activist George Clooney on behalf of his organization at its annual dinner in New York.[[86]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Walter_Cronkite#cite_note-86)

Chunks: 0,1,2
Victor Sidney Norton was the elder son of Sidney (Peter) Norton, a Johannesburg journalist, and his wife. His father's descent was English and his mother was of Swedish extraction.
Norton's limited formal education was enriched by exposure to his father's lively mind and wide reading. Among his varied experiences after he had left school was a spell behind the counter of a store in Duiwelskloof in the former North Eastern Transvaal. Here, characteristically, he spent rainy days studying Mathematics from textbooks found in a storeroom.
In 1927 he joined The Star as a reporter. He was soon transferred to the Bulawayo Chronicle in what was then Southern Rhodesia. By this time he had become an exceptionally skilled self taught shorthand writer.
In 1931he and a fellow reporter, Bob Crisp (later famous as a cricketer and a much decorated soldier of the Second World War), made their way to Cape Town with the idea of earning their passage to South America on a cattle ship. When this plan was thwarted by an outbreak of foot and mouth disease, both found jobs on the _Cape Times_.
Norton's outstanding ability was soon noticed by the editor, B.K. Long*, and he was assigned to Parliament as writer of 'Notes in the House', a column with considerable prestige. Parliament fascinated him, and he made himself an acknowledged authority on its rules and procedures.
In 1935, after short periods as chief subeditor, leader writer and chief of editorial staff, he became chief assistant editor under Long's successor, G.H. Wilson. When Wilson retired in 1944, Norton, though only 37, succeeded him. He was the first South African born editor of the _Cape Times_ and among the first South Africans to edit any of the country's major English language newspapers.
His brand of journalism was highly personal, combining strong political convictions, vigorously expressed in leading articles, with an iron insistence on accurate, fair and responsible reporting. No news story, he maintained, was, fit for publication unless it included the 'other side'.
Scarcely less strenuous was his concern for good English. He was himself a master of the language and wrote with remarkable facility. His leaders, forceful, eloquent and polished, were typed at top speed, usually with scarcely a note to guide him.

If his judgements were not always free from prejudice or oversimplification, they at least left no one in doubt as to where he and his newspaper stood.
Perhaps the most notable period of Norton's editorship was the 1950s, when the _Cape Times_ threw itself into the battle against the wave of legislation that removed coloured voters in the Cape from the Common Roll. It was issues of this kind, involving questions of justice and human rights, that stirred him most and evoked leading articles that have been described as'like the crack of a long whip'.
His courage was demonstrated by his repeated readiness to risk an action for defamation rather than withhold any criticism that he believed justified and necessary. Yet he remained on good personal terms with many of those he lashed so mercilessly in his leading articles. On his death, a former editor of _Die Burger_, Dr Piet Cillie, paid tribute to him as an outstanding newspaper man and a worthy antagonist who 'never let our public differences damage our personal relations'. It was on Norton's initiative, he recalled, that the Cape Times and Die Burger began the practice of printing each other's main leaders.
In 1960 Norton was called to the Bar of the Senate the first South African editor to be so summoned to be reprimanded for contempt of Parliament. This followed the finding of a Select Committee that he had committed a breach of privilege by publishing (albeit without comment), words used by a Member of Parliament, Mr J. Hamilton Russell, about the enlarged Senate.
He attended conferences of the Commonwealth Press Union in Britain and Australia and was for 12 years Chairperson of the South African Morning Newspaper Group, an organization for the exchange of news. He retired in 1971. Two years later Rhodes University in Grahamstown awarded him an Honorary Doctorate in Literature.
Norton's editorial combativeness concealed a genial and generous personality, with much humour, an unfeigned enjoyment of life and much goodwill towards all he met.
One of the many things he was enthusiastic about was French, which, with his usual tenacity, he learned to speak fluently. He read extensively in French literature and made an exhaustive study of the phonetics of that language.
Of medium height, strongly built, he revelled in outdoor pursuits. He was a keen yachtsman and played a key role in the organization of successive Atlantic yacht races.

In 1935 Norton married Mildred Elizabeth Mary (Molly) McClurg, with whom he shared a tireless social life and a wide circle of friends. Their daughters, Tessa Clark and Judy Olivier, both became journalists.

Title: New Orleans’ secret hangover cure
Chunks: 0,1,2,3
Site search
30 May 2018
Amanda Ruggeri Features correspondent
Amanda Ruggeri
Known as ‘Old Sober’, yakamein is a popular cure for hangovers in New Orleans (Credit: Amanda Ruggeri)
**Affectionately dubbed ‘Old Sober’, the little-known New Orleans dish called yakamein is said to right even the worst symptoms of fun.**
On a recent Sunday afternoon, Frenchmen Street was relatively tranquil. People still were sleeping off the night before or finishing up late-day brunches to quell any lingering after-effects. Strains of jazz – an accordion, clarinet, tuba – leaked onto the street. Rainbow-bright clapboard houses competed with the brilliant blue of the sky.
But the most New Orleans detail of all was the paper cup I was holding. No, it wasn’t a hurricane, that noxiously sweet rum cocktail every tourist sips through a straw at least once during their visit. It was the opposite: a remedy, affectionately dubbed ‘Old Sober’, said to right even the worst symptoms of fun.
Despite how I’d been served it, it wasn’t a drink. It was a soup – sort of. More spaghetti than broth, this version was heady and potent, kicked up with a triple Sriracha-Crystal hot sauce-Tabasco threat, and laden with juicy, coin-sized chunks of alligator meat. Of the latter, New Orleans native Linda Green, better known as Ms Linda the Yakamein Lady, put it best: “He look like a mean character, but he's a beautiful piece of meat and a delicious piece of meat.”
Amanda Ruggeri
Known as ‘Old Sober’, yakamein is a popular cure for hangovers in New Orleans (Credit: Amanda Ruggeri)
**You may also be interested in:**
Yakamein (pronounced ‘YAH-kah-main’) is one of those foods that, if you weren’t born and bred in New Orleans, you’re sure you’ve never heard of in your life. And then, with equal certainty, you suddenly know you can’t live without it ever again. But live without it most of us must.

Yes, it sounds simple enough to make at home – especially as the most common version uses beef, a useful alternative if you, like me, don’t have easy access to alligator (something that very much surprised Ms Linda when I told her). Boil leftover cuts of beef (extra authenticity points if they come from a Sunday roast cooked for family and friends). Simmer with salt, black pepper and garlic powder. Layer cooked spaghetti, tender bits of beef, chopped green onion and a boiled egg in a bowl or cup. Pour on the broth, give it a shake and let the flavours meld. Add extra hot sauce, if you want. Presto: yakamein.
When you taste yakamein, you come back to life
But like any fiercely local dish, yakamein almost doesn’t make sense outside of New Orleans. And not just because it’s both answer and antidote to the city’s fun-loving (and drink-swilling) attitude. It’s also that its flavours are brewed from the Big Easy’s multicultural web, and its cup-and-slurp style speaks to the city’s warm, down-home lack of pretension.
The dish’s legendary status even plays, in part, on the city’s black magic beliefs – because ‘Old Sober’ is more than a cute name.
“Sometimes, you know, you just out of it. But when you taste yakamein, believe it or not, you come back to life,” said Ms Linda. “My daughter, she might go out with her girlfriends, and she’ll come in in the morning – _Maaaa, I need a yakamein. Maaaa, I need a yakamein._ And I _have_ to go get it.”
Amanda Ruggeri
Yakamein’s flavours are brewed from New Orleans’ multicultural web, thought to be a fusion of Chinese and African-American cuisine (Credit: Amanda Ruggeri)
Like so much in New Orleans, yakamein is a hodgepodge and, because it’s a hodgepodge, difficult to investigate. “Nobody can pinpoint exactly where it came from,” said New Orleans native John Bel, one of a growing number of chefs to offer yakamein on the menu at his upscale restaurant Meauxbar.

It’s thought to be a fusion that resulted when Chinese immigrants and African-Americans blended homes, kitchens and ingredients in the early 1900s. But others say it developed further after World War II, or maybe the Vietnam and Korean Wars, when soldiers returned from the Pacific Theatre with memories of hot noodle soups.
Yakamein almost doesn’t make sense outside of New Orleans
Adding to the confusion is that there are yakamein-like soups elsewhere. Pho has similarities. So does ramen. And you’d be forgiven for thinking the closest variant, which hails from south-eastern Virginia, might even be the exact same thing. After all, it’s called yock – short for yock-a-mein. But yock-a-mein comes in a Chinese take-out box. It uses lo-mein egg noodles, not spaghetti, and often features sausage and white onions, which yakamein does not. Instead of hot sauce, ketchup is key, vinegar optional. Chinese immigrants may have played a role in developing Virginia’s version too, but the dish itself looks – and tastes – altogether different.
And so, except for die-hard foodies or fans of Anthony Bourdain’s No Reservations (which featured Ms Linda in 2011), yakamein is little known outside of New Orleans. When I mentioned to a couple of Baton Rouge residents that I was writing a story about yakamein, they had no idea what I was talking about.
“Very few visitors have heard of it. Some people, when they’re a foodie or are in New Orleans to eat, they’ve at least heard of it – but they don’t quite understand what it is,” Bel said.
Amanda Ruggeri
Affectionately known as the Yakamein Lady, Ms Linda Green dishes out cups of yakamein from the back of her pick-up truck (Credit: Amanda Ruggeri)
What everyone agrees on, though, is that no matter who began cooking yakamein or exactly when, it came from family kitchens and the streets. As well as being made at home, yakamein was sold outside jazz bars and on the sides of second lines, the parades of dancing, singing celebrants that got their start as funeral celebrations.

This, as well as New Orleans’ general lack of pretension, also explains the local etiquette for eating yakamein: other than slurping it down in someone’s kitchen, the most authentic way to enjoy it is in a to-go container. Spoons not only aren’t required, they’d be a hindrance.
Bel’s version of yakamein, served up at Meauxbar, came from similarly down-home roots. One of the prep cooks used to bring yakamein to the restaurant for her lunch. Then she started sharing it with the staff. Then making it at staff meals. It didn’t take long for the recipe to wind up on the menu, where now it’s a daily favourite.
Meauxbar’s yakamein is good: layered with the umami of soy sauce, a heavy hand of celery and a dash of Worcestershire, it’s made of more broth than others. (Partly for that reason, partly because of the upscale bistro surroundings, I used a spoon for this one – or tried to).
Madison Sanders/Madison Sanders Photography
Meauxbar began serving yakamein after one of its prep cooks shared her version with the restaurant staff (Credit: Madison Sanders/Madison Sanders Photography)
But later, when I think of New Orleans yakamein, it’s Ms Linda’s version I remember. I’m not alone. Ms Linda is famed for dishing out thousands of cups of yakamein out of the back of her pick-up truck at second lines, the French Market, Jazz Fest and Mardi Gras. (Word to the wise: if you are going to ask Ms Linda how much yakamein she sells each Jazz Fest, don’t do it while you have a mouth full of yakamein. “Oooh. Oh my God. There’s a lot. It’s a _lot_. It’s over – 25,000?” Cue me spluttering soup. “Oh, don’t choke!”). Ms Linda cooks everything: etouffee and gumbo and jambalaya and beignets. But the recipe that she learned from her mamma, who learned it from her mamma, is yakamein.

## The Irony of Korea’s Hangover Cure: It Makes You Want More Drinks
9 min read
Nov 21, 2025
Press enter or click to view image in full size
A Bloody Mary with pomegranate juice. The best thing in my life. | Photo by author. No reuse without permission

## The Most Dangerous Bloody Mary I Ever Had
One autumn evening, I attended a whisky tasting class in my role as a food editor. It was a unique session where a vegetable sommelier and whisky ambassador taught us how to pair vegetables and fruits with whisky. And there, as an aperitif, I encountered the most delicious Bloody Mary I’d ever tasted.
I never liked the raw, vegetal taste of tomato juice in cocktails, so I was shocked — how could this drink taste so much like a tomato, and yet so much like a fruit at the same time? When I asked the bartender, who had clearly put thought into crafting vegetable-based cocktails for this occasion, the secret turned out to be pomegranate juice.
Ah, so that was it! The rich, sweet pomegranate juice wrapped around the tomato’s vegetable-ness, bringing out its fruit-like qualities. Anyone drinking this would probably settle the “is tomato a fruit or vegetable?” debate firmly on the fruit side. Lost in this thought, I happily gulped down two glasses of this pomegranate Bloody Mary, and only when my vision started to swim did I realize: this Bloody Mary contained a generous amount of Glenfiddich whisky — the star of the tasting class.
Wait, wasn’t the Bloody Mary supposed to be a hangover-**cure** cocktail? What if I get drunk from drinking it? Oh, right — a hangover cure _cocktail_.
Imagine that: getting drunk from a drink meant to cure the effects of drinking. But I’m actually quite familiar with this ironic concept. We have it in Korea, too. Food meant for hangover recovery that actually calls for more drinking. Food that makes you suspect it became a hangover cure simply because drinkers loved it. Food that literally has “hangover cure” in its name: haejangguk (해장국).
Press enter or click to view image in full size
Cheongjinok’s Haejangguk. Eat it with the chili seasoning on the side mixed in. | Photo by author. No reuse without permission

## Literally “Korean Hangover Cure Soup”
Haejangguk. _Haejang_ means “hangover cure” in Korean, and _guk_ means “soup.” So the name itself literally means “soup for curing hangovers.”
Koreans have always loved soup-based dishes. In fact, there’s even a disparaging phrase for a high-maintenance husband — “someone who can’t eat rice without soup.” Rice with soup, a few side dishes, and kimchi — that’s the basic structure of a Korean meal.
So on those miserable mornings when the good feelings from last night’s drinking have evaporated and all that’s left is a churning stomach, turning to a hot soup dish for comfort — like chicken soup for the soul — is perhaps the most naturally Korean response.
Visit a restaurant famous for haejangguk in the morning. You’ll see middle-aged men whose faces clearly show last night’s drinking, pouring rice into their bubbling earthenware bowls of haejangguk and sweating profusely as they eat, exclaiming, “This is the stuff!” It’s like taking a sauna while eating. Then, once their stomachs settle a bit and the spicy broth lifts their spirits, there’s always someone who orders alcohol as a side drink.
Sir! If you want to detox from the alcohol, you shouldn’t be drinking more!
But it can’t be helped. Drinkers eat a lot of haejangguk because it’s the flavor profile drinkers love, and naturally, foods that drinkers love call for more drinking. At this point, you start to wonder if it’s even ironic that haejangguk leads to more drinking.
Press enter or click to view image in full size
Boiling pots of haejangguk side by side | Photo by author. No reuse without permission

## Understanding Korean Spicy Hangovers as You Age
When I first reached the legal drinking age and was busy testing my limits, I couldn’t understand these men eating haejangguk first thing in the morning. My stomach was churning, everything felt like it would come back up, and yet they were eating such heavy food? My hangover cure back then was usually fresh tomato juice — not from a can, but actually blended from real tomatoes. Or I’d try pizza or hamburgers, having heard that’s what college students overseas did.
But after two decades of drinking, I finally understand the men who order haejangguk the next morning. You have to have a slightly damaged stomach to appreciate it. Most modern Koreans — stressed, caffeinated, and overworked — have fragile stomachs. After a night of drinking, your once gentle pink stomach feels shredded. And like an itch on rough skin, only a good scratch brings relief — that scratch, for Koreans, is the fiery, spicy heat of haejangguk. It burns, it soothes, and somehow it heals.
Press enter or click to view image in full size
Sliced beef offal and soybean sprouts generously added to haejangguk | Photo by author. No reuse without permission

## The Haejangguk Street of Seoul
If you want to experience the most Korean-style hangover cure, head to Cheongjin-dong in downtown Seoul — a street that used to be filled with haejangguk restaurants. One of its most famous restaurants, _Cheongjinok_, dates back to 1937, when a grandmother first set up a cauldron on the street to sell soup to early risers. The third generation still runs it today.
Haejangguk is an old dish with a long and layered history. Sometimes the term is used loosely to describe any hot soup eaten to ease a hangover, but in its original form, haejangguk refers to a hearty beef-broth soup made with beef offal, chili flakes, dried radish greens (ugeoji), soybean sprouts (kongnamul), and congealed ox blood (seonji).
As these basic ingredients suggest, haejangguk originated in the alleyways near the palace, where beef — a precious ingredient — was available. While the king and court officials traveled along the main boulevards, workers and merchants passed through the side streets and alleys. There, vendors used the relatively cheap, leftover beef offal and blood to create an accessible, nutritious meal for these laborers. That’s why it’s located in Cheongjin-dong, in the alley right next to Jongno’s main road, and why it uses beef byproducts and affordable, easily available vegetables.
Press enter or click to view image in full size
Cheongjinok’s massive cauldron of haejangguk with seonji and napa cabbage | Photo by author. No reuse without permission

## Haejangguk in History
In the past, Korea had a curfew system — no one could be on the streets from midnight until 4 a.m. At 4 a.m. on the dot, people would flock to these Cheongjin-dong haejangguk restaurants to settle their stomachs. After the curfew was abolished, the restaurants became even more packed — customers who’d been drinking all night, customers who’d have a drink after eating haejangguk — there was barely room to stand, I heard. That’s why, until the COVID pandemic, many haejangguk restaurants in Korea operated 24 hours.

## Get Yeonjoo Jung’s stories in your inbox
Join Medium for free to get updates from this writer.
Remember me for faster sign in
As you can tell from the ingredients, this type of haejangguk is best when made in large batches and simmered for a long time. If you ever get a chance to peek into Cheongjinok’s fourth-floor kitchen, you’ll see two enormous cauldrons — big enough to swallow the sun — bubbling away side by side. The broth is made by simmering beef offal, beef leg bones, and brisket for hours, then adding seonji and other vegetables to create a spicy haejangguk that pairs perfectly with soju.
If you were to name a traditional food for common people, a quintessentially Seoul dish for ordinary folks, haejangguk would certainly make the list. According to records, the first delivery food in the Joseon Dynasty was also a predecessor of this traditional haejangguk — _hyojong-gaeng_ was delivered to wealthy homes for hangover relief.

30 May 2018
Amanda Ruggeri Features correspondent
Amanda Ruggeri
Known as ‘Old Sober’, yakamein is a popular cure for hangovers in New Orleans (Credit: Amanda Ruggeri)
**Affectionately dubbed ‘Old Sober’, the little-known New Orleans dish called yakamein is said to right even the worst symptoms of fun.**
On a recent Sunday afternoon, Frenchmen Street was relatively tranquil. People still were sleeping off the night before or finishing up late-day brunches to quell any lingering after-effects. Strains of jazz – an accordion, clarinet, tuba – leaked onto the street. Rainbow-bright clapboard houses competed with the brilliant blue of the sky.
But the most New Orleans detail of all was the paper cup I was holding. No, it wasn’t a hurricane, that noxiously sweet rum cocktail every tourist sips through a straw at least once during their visit. It was the opposite: a remedy, affectionately dubbed ‘Old Sober’, said to right even the worst symptoms of fun.
Despite how I’d been served it, it wasn’t a drink. It was a soup – sort of. More spaghetti than broth, this version was heady and potent, kicked up with a triple Sriracha-Crystal hot sauce-Tabasco threat, and laden with juicy, coin-sized chunks of alligator meat. Of the latter, New Orleans native Linda Green, better known as Ms Linda the Yakamein Lady, put it best: “He look like a mean character, but he's a beautiful piece of meat and a delicious piece of meat.”
Amanda Ruggeri
Known as ‘Old Sober’, yakamein is a popular cure for hangovers in New Orleans (Credit: Amanda Ruggeri)
**You may also be interested in:**
Yakamein (pronounced ‘YAH-kah-main’) is one of those foods that, if you weren’t born and bred in New Orleans, you’re sure you’ve never heard of in your life. And then, with equal certainty, you suddenly know you can’t live without it ever again. But live without it most of us must.
texts.1:
Yes, it sounds simple enough to make at home – especially as the most common version uses beef, a useful alternative if you, like me, don’t have easy access to alligator (something that very much surprised Ms Linda when I told her). Boil leftover cuts of beef (extra authenticity points if they come from a Sunday roast cooked for family and friends). Simmer with salt, black pepper and garlic powder. Layer cooked spaghetti, tender bits of beef, chopped green onion and a boiled egg in a bowl or cup. Pour on the broth, give it a shake and let the flavours meld. Add extra hot sauce, if you want. Presto: yakamein.
When you taste yakamein, you come back to life
But like any fiercely local dish, yakamein almost doesn’t make sense outside of New Orleans. And not just because it’s both answer and antidote to the city’s fun-loving (and drink-swilling) attitude. It’s also that its flavours are brewed from the Big Easy’s multicultural web, and its cup-and-slurp style speaks to the city’s warm, down-home lack of pretension.
The dish’s legendary status even plays, in part, on the city’s black magic beliefs – because ‘Old Sober’ is more than a cute name.
“Sometimes, you know, you just out of it. But when you taste yakamein, believe it or not, you come back to life,” said Ms Linda. “My daughter, she might go out with her girlfriends, and she’ll come in in the morning – _Maaaa, I need a yakamein. Maaaa, I need a yakamein._ And I _have_ to go get it.”
Amanda Ruggeri
Yakamein’s flavours are brewed from New Orleans’ multicultural web, thought to be a fusion of Chinese and African-American cuisine (Credit: Amanda Ruggeri)
Like so much in New Orleans, yakamein is a hodgepodge and, because it’s a hodgepodge, difficult to investigate. “Nobody can pinpoint exactly where it came from,” said New Orleans native John Bel, one of a growing number of chefs to offer yakamein on the menu at his upscale restaurant Meauxbar.
texts.2:
It’s thought to be a fusion that resulted when Chinese immigrants and African-Americans blended homes, kitchens and ingredients in the early 1900s. But others say it developed further after World War II, or maybe the Vietnam and Korean Wars, when soldiers returned from the Pacific Theatre with memories of hot noodle soups.
Yakamein almost doesn’t make sense outside of New Orleans
Adding to the confusion is that there are yakamein-like soups elsewhere. Pho has similarities. So does ramen. And you’d be forgiven for thinking the closest variant, which hails from south-eastern Virginia, might even be the exact same thing. After all, it’s called yock – short for yock-a-mein. But yock-a-mein comes in a Chinese take-out box. It uses lo-mein egg noodles, not spaghetti, and often features sausage and white onions, which yakamein does not. Instead of hot sauce, ketchup is key, vinegar optional. Chinese immigrants may have played a role in developing Virginia’s version too, but the dish itself looks – and tastes – altogether different.
And so, except for die-hard foodies or fans of Anthony Bourdain’s No Reservations (which featured Ms Linda in 2011), yakamein is little known outside of New Orleans. When I mentioned to a couple of Baton Rouge residents that I was writing a story about yakamein, they had no idea what I was talking about.
“Very few visitors have heard of it. Some people, when they’re a foodie or are in New Orleans to eat, they’ve at least heard of it – but they don’t quite understand what it is,” Bel said.
Amanda Ruggeri
Affectionately known as the Yakamein Lady, Ms Linda Green dishes out cups of yakamein from the back of her pick-up truck (Credit: Amanda Ruggeri)
What everyone agrees on, though, is that no matter who began cooking yakamein or exactly when, it came from family kitchens and the streets. As well as being made at home, yakamein was sold outside jazz bars and on the sides of second lines, the parades of dancing, singing celebrants that got their start as funeral celebrations.
texts.3:
This, as well as New Orleans’ general lack of pretension, also explains the local etiquette for eating yakamein: other than slurping it down in someone’s kitchen, the most authentic way to enjoy it is in a to-go container. Spoons not only aren’t required, they’d be a hindrance.
Bel’s version of yakamein, served up at Meauxbar, came from similarly down-home roots. One of the prep cooks used to bring yakamein to the restaurant for her lunch. Then she started sharing it with the staff. Then making it at staff meals. It didn’t take long for the recipe to wind up on the menu, where now it’s a daily favourite.
Meauxbar’s yakamein is good: layered with the umami of soy sauce, a heavy hand of celery and a dash of Worcestershire, it’s made of more broth than others. (Partly for that reason, partly because of the upscale bistro surroundings, I used a spoon for this one – or tried to).
Madison Sanders/Madison Sanders Photography
Meauxbar began serving yakamein after one of its prep cooks shared her version with the restaurant staff (Credit: Madison Sanders/Madison Sanders Photography)
But later, when I think of New Orleans yakamein, it’s Ms Linda’s version I remember. I’m not alone. Ms Linda is famed for dishing out thousands of cups of yakamein out of the back of her pick-up truck at second lines, the French Market, Jazz Fest and Mardi Gras. (Word to the wise: if you are going to ask Ms Linda how much yakamein she sells each Jazz Fest, don’t do it while you have a mouth full of yakamein. “Oooh. Oh my God. There’s a lot. It’s a _lot_. It’s over – 25,000?” Cue me spluttering soup. “Oh, don’t choke!”). Ms Linda cooks everything: etouffee and gumbo and jambalaya and beignets. But the recipe that she learned from her mamma, who learned it from her mamma, is yakamein.

Or I’d try pizza or hamburgers, having heard that’s what college students overseas did.
But after two decades of drinking, I finally understand the men who order haejangguk the next morning. You have to have a slightly damaged stomach to appreciate it. Most modern Koreans — stressed, caffeinated, and overworked — have fragile stomachs. After a night of drinking, your once gentle pink stomach feels shredded. And like an itch on rough skin, only a good scratch brings relief — that scratch, for Koreans, is the fiery, spicy heat of haejangguk. It burns, it soothes, and somehow it heals.

## The Haejangguk Street of Seoul
If you want to experience the most Korean-style hangover cure, head to Cheongjin-dong in downtown Seoul — a street that used to be filled with haejangguk restaurants. One of its most famous restaurants, _Cheongjinok_, dates back to 1937, when a grandmother first set up a cauldron on the street to sell soup to early risers. The third generation still runs it today.
Haejangguk is an old dish with a long and layered history. Sometimes the term is used loosely to describe any hot soup eaten to ease a hangover, but in its original form, haejangguk refers to a hearty beef-broth soup made with beef offal, chili flakes, dried radish greens (ugeoji), soybean sprouts (kongnamul), and congealed ox blood (seonji).
As these basic ingredients suggest, haejangguk originated in the alleyways near the palace, where beef — a precious ingredient — was available. While the king and court officials traveled along the main boulevards, workers and merchants passed through the side streets and alleys. There, vendors used the relatively cheap, leftover beef offal and blood to create an accessible, nutritious meal for these laborers. That’s why it’s located in Cheongjin-dong, in the alley right next to Jongno’s main road, and why it uses beef byproducts and affordable, easily available vegetables.
Press enter or click to view image in full size
Cheongjinok’s massive cauldron of haejangguk with seonji and napa cabbage | Photo by author. No reuse without permission
texts.6:
## Haejangguk in History
In the past, Korea had a curfew system — no one could be on the streets from midnight until 4 a.m. At 4 a.m. on the dot, people would flock to these Cheongjin-dong haejangguk restaurants to settle their stomachs. After the curfew was abolished, the restaurants became even more packed — customers who’d been drinking all night, customers who’d have a drink after eating haejangguk — there was barely room to stand, I heard. That’s why, until the COVID pandemic, many haejangguk restaurants in Korea operated 24 hours.
texts.7:
## Get Yeonjoo Jung’s stories in your inbox
Join Medium for free to get updates from this writer.
Remember me for faster sign in
As you can tell from the ingredients, this type of haejangguk is best when made in large batches and simmered for a long time. If you ever get a chance to peek into Cheongjinok’s fourth-floor kitchen, you’ll see two enormous cauldrons — big enough to swallow the sun — bubbling away side by side. The broth is made by simmering beef offal, beef leg bones, and brisket for hours, then adding seonji and other vegetables to create a spicy haejangguk that pairs perfectly with soju.
If you were to name a traditional food for common people, a quintessentially Seoul dish for ordinary folks, haejangguk would certainly make the list. According to records, the first delivery food in the Joseon Dynasty was also a predecessor of this traditional haejangguk — _hyojong-gaeng_ was delivered to wealthy homes for hangover relief.

Title: New Orleans’ secret hangover cure
Chunks: 0,1,2,3
Site search
30 May 2018
Amanda Ruggeri Features correspondent
Amanda Ruggeri
Known as ‘Old Sober’, yakamein is a popular cure for hangovers in New Orleans (Credit: Amanda Ruggeri)
**Affectionately dubbed ‘Old Sober’, the little-known New Orleans dish called yakamein is said to right even the worst symptoms of fun.**
On a recent Sunday afternoon, Frenchmen Street was relatively tranquil. People still were sleeping off the night before or finishing up late-day brunches to quell any lingering after-effects. Strains of jazz – an accordion, clarinet, tuba – leaked onto the street. Rainbow-bright clapboard houses competed with the brilliant blue of the sky.
But the most New Orleans detail of all was the paper cup I was holding. No, it wasn’t a hurricane, that noxiously sweet rum cocktail every tourist sips through a straw at least once during their visit. It was the opposite: a remedy, affectionately dubbed ‘Old Sober’, said to right even the worst symptoms of fun.
Despite how I’d been served it, it wasn’t a drink. It was a soup – sort of. More spaghetti than broth, this version was heady and potent, kicked up with a triple Sriracha-Crystal hot sauce-Tabasco threat, and laden with juicy, coin-sized chunks of alligator meat. Of the latter, New Orleans native Linda Green, better known as Ms Linda the Yakamein Lady, put it best: “He look like a mean character, but he's a beautiful piece of meat and a delicious piece of meat.”
Amanda Ruggeri
Known as ‘Old Sober’, yakamein is a popular cure for hangovers in New Orleans (Credit: Amanda Ruggeri)
**You may also be interested in:**
Yakamein (pronounced ‘YAH-kah-main’) is one of those foods that, if you weren’t born and bred in New Orleans, you’re sure you’ve never heard of in your life. And then, with equal certainty, you suddenly know you can’t live without it ever again. But live without it most of us must.

Yes, it sounds simple enough to make at home – especially as the most common version uses beef, a useful alternative if you, like me, don’t have easy access to alligator (something that very much surprised Ms Linda when I told her). Boil leftover cuts of beef (extra authenticity points if they come from a Sunday roast cooked for family and friends). Simmer with salt, black pepper and garlic powder. Layer cooked spaghetti, tender bits of beef, chopped green onion and a boiled egg in a bowl or cup. Pour on the broth, give it a shake and let the flavours meld. Add extra hot sauce, if you want. Presto: yakamein.
When you taste yakamein, you come back to life
But like any fiercely local dish, yakamein almost doesn’t make sense outside of New Orleans. And not just because it’s both answer and antidote to the city’s fun-loving (and drink-swilling) attitude. It’s also that its flavours are brewed from the Big Easy’s multicultural web, and its cup-and-slurp style speaks to the city’s warm, down-home lack of pretension.
The dish’s legendary status even plays, in part, on the city’s black magic beliefs – because ‘Old Sober’ is more than a cute name.
“Sometimes, you know, you just out of it. But when you taste yakamein, believe it or not, you come back to life,” said Ms Linda. “My daughter, she might go out with her girlfriends, and she’ll come in in the morning – _Maaaa, I need a yakamein. Maaaa, I need a yakamein._ And I _have_ to go get it.”
Amanda Ruggeri
Yakamein’s flavours are brewed from New Orleans’ multicultural web, thought to be a fusion of Chinese and African-American cuisine (Credit: Amanda Ruggeri)
Like so much in New Orleans, yakamein is a hodgepodge and, because it’s a hodgepodge, difficult to investigate. “Nobody can pinpoint exactly where it came from,” said New Orleans native John Bel, one of a growing number of chefs to offer yakamein on the menu at his upscale restaurant Meauxbar.

It’s thought to be a fusion that resulted when Chinese immigrants and African-Americans blended homes, kitchens and ingredients in the early 1900s. But others say it developed further after World War II, or maybe the Vietnam and Korean Wars, when soldiers returned from the Pacific Theatre with memories of hot noodle soups.
Yakamein almost doesn’t make sense outside of New Orleans
Adding to the confusion is that there are yakamein-like soups elsewhere. Pho has similarities. So does ramen. And you’d be forgiven for thinking the closest variant, which hails from south-eastern Virginia, might even be the exact same thing. After all, it’s called yock – short for yock-a-mein. But yock-a-mein comes in a Chinese take-out box. It uses lo-mein egg noodles, not spaghetti, and often features sausage and white onions, which yakamein does not. Instead of hot sauce, ketchup is key, vinegar optional. Chinese immigrants may have played a role in developing Virginia’s version too, but the dish itself looks – and tastes – altogether different.
And so, except for die-hard foodies or fans of Anthony Bourdain’s No Reservations (which featured Ms Linda in 2011), yakamein is little known outside of New Orleans. When I mentioned to a couple of Baton Rouge residents that I was writing a story about yakamein, they had no idea what I was talking about.
“Very few visitors have heard of it. Some people, when they’re a foodie or are in New Orleans to eat, they’ve at least heard of it – but they don’t quite understand what it is,” Bel said.
Amanda Ruggeri
Affectionately known as the Yakamein Lady, Ms Linda Green dishes out cups of yakamein from the back of her pick-up truck (Credit: Amanda Ruggeri)
What everyone agrees on, though, is that no matter who began cooking yakamein or exactly when, it came from family kitchens and the streets. As well as being made at home, yakamein was sold outside jazz bars and on the sides of second lines, the parades of dancing, singing celebrants that got their start as funeral celebrations.

This, as well as New Orleans’ general lack of pretension, also explains the local etiquette for eating yakamein: other than slurping it down in someone’s kitchen, the most authentic way to enjoy it is in a to-go container. Spoons not only aren’t required, they’d be a hindrance.
Bel’s version of yakamein, served up at Meauxbar, came from similarly down-home roots. One of the prep cooks used to bring yakamein to the restaurant for her lunch. Then she started sharing it with the staff. Then making it at staff meals. It didn’t take long for the recipe to wind up on the menu, where now it’s a daily favourite.
Meauxbar’s yakamein is good: layered with the umami of soy sauce, a heavy hand of celery and a dash of Worcestershire, it’s made of more broth than others. (Partly for that reason, partly because of the upscale bistro surroundings, I used a spoon for this one – or tried to).
Madison Sanders/Madison Sanders Photography
Meauxbar began serving yakamein after one of its prep cooks shared her version with the restaurant staff (Credit: Madison Sanders/Madison Sanders Photography)
But later, when I think of New Orleans yakamein, it’s Ms Linda’s version I remember. I’m not alone. Ms Linda is famed for dishing out thousands of cups of yakamein out of the back of her pick-up truck at second lines, the French Market, Jazz Fest and Mardi Gras. (Word to the wise: if you are going to ask Ms Linda how much yakamein she sells each Jazz Fest, don’t do it while you have a mouth full of yakamein. “Oooh. Oh my God. There’s a lot. It’s a _lot_. It’s over – 25,000?” Cue me spluttering soup. “Oh, don’t choke!”). Ms Linda cooks everything: etouffee and gumbo and jambalaya and beignets. But the recipe that she learned from her mamma, who learned it from her mamma, is yakamein.

## The Irony of Korea’s Hangover Cure: It Makes You Want More Drinks
9 min read
Nov 21, 2025
Press enter or click to view image in full size
A Bloody Mary with pomegranate juice. The best thing in my life. | Photo by author. No reuse without permission

## The Most Dangerous Bloody Mary I Ever Had
One autumn evening, I attended a whisky tasting class in my role as a food editor. It was a unique session where a vegetable sommelier and whisky ambassador taught us how to pair vegetables and fruits with whisky. And there, as an aperitif, I encountered the most delicious Bloody Mary I’d ever tasted.
I never liked the raw, vegetal taste of tomato juice in cocktails, so I was shocked — how could this drink taste so much like a tomato, and yet so much like a fruit at the same time? When I asked the bartender, who had clearly put thought into crafting vegetable-based cocktails for this occasion, the secret turned out to be pomegranate juice.
Ah, so that was it! The rich, sweet pomegranate juice wrapped around the tomato’s vegetable-ness, bringing out its fruit-like qualities. Anyone drinking this would probably settle the “is tomato a fruit or vegetable?” debate firmly on the fruit side. Lost in this thought, I happily gulped down two glasses of this pomegranate Bloody Mary, and only when my vision started to swim did I realize: this Bloody Mary contained a generous amount of Glenfiddich whisky — the star of the tasting class.
Wait, wasn’t the Bloody Mary supposed to be a hangover-**cure** cocktail? What if I get drunk from drinking it? Oh, right — a hangover cure _cocktail_.
Imagine that: getting drunk from a drink meant to cure the effects of drinking. But I’m actually quite familiar with this ironic concept. We have it in Korea, too. Food meant for hangover recovery that actually calls for more drinking. Food that makes you suspect it became a hangover cure simply because drinkers loved it. Food that literally has “hangover cure” in its name: haejangguk (해장국).
Press enter or click to view image in full size

## Literally “Korean Hangover Cure Soup”
Haejangguk. _Haejang_ means “hangover cure” in Korean, and _guk_ means “soup.” So the name itself literally means “soup for curing hangovers.”
Koreans have always loved soup-based dishes. In fact, there’s even a disparaging phrase for a high-maintenance husband — “someone who can’t eat rice without soup.” Rice with soup, a few side dishes, and kimchi — that’s the basic structure of a Korean meal.
So on those miserable mornings when the good feelings from last night’s drinking have evaporated and all that’s left is a churning stomach, turning to a hot soup dish for comfort — like chicken soup for the soul — is perhaps the most naturally Korean response.
Visit a restaurant famous for haejangguk in the morning. You’ll see middle-aged men whose faces clearly show last night’s drinking, pouring rice into their bubbling earthenware bowls of haejangguk and sweating profusely as they eat, exclaiming, “This is the stuff!” It’s like taking a sauna while eating. Then, once their stomachs settle a bit and the spicy broth lifts their spirits, there’s always someone who orders alcohol as a side drink.
Sir! If you want to detox from the alcohol, you shouldn’t be drinking more!
But it can’t be helped. Drinkers eat a lot of haejangguk because it’s the flavor profile drinkers love, and naturally, foods that drinkers love call for more drinking. At this point, you start to wonder if it’s even ironic that haejangguk leads to more drinking.
Press enter or click to view image in full size
