## Understanding Korean Spicy Hangovers as You Age
When I first reached the legal drinking age and was busy testing my limits, I couldn’t understand these men eating haejangguk first thing in the morning. My stomach was churning, everything felt like it would come back up, and yet they were eating such heavy food? My hangover cure back then was usually fresh tomato juice — not from a can, but actually blended from real tomatoes. Or I’d try pizza or hamburgers, having heard that’s what college students overseas did.
But after two decades of drinking, I finally understand the men who order haejangguk the next morning. You have to have a slightly damaged stomach to appreciate it. Most modern Koreans — stressed, caffeinated, and overworked — have fragile stomachs. After a night of drinking, your once gentle pink stomach feels shredded. And like an itch on rough skin, only a good scratch brings relief — that scratch, for Koreans, is the fiery, spicy heat of haejangguk. It burns, it soothes, and somehow it heals.

## The Haejangguk Street of Seoul
If you want to experience the most Korean-style hangover cure, head to Cheongjin-dong in downtown Seoul — a street that used to be filled with haejangguk restaurants. One of its most famous restaurants, _Cheongjinok_, dates back to 1937, when a grandmother first set up a cauldron on the street to sell soup to early risers. The third generation still runs it today.
Haejangguk is an old dish with a long and layered history. Sometimes the term is used loosely to describe any hot soup eaten to ease a hangover, but in its original form, haejangguk refers to a hearty beef-broth soup made with beef offal, chili flakes, dried radish greens (ugeoji), soybean sprouts (kongnamul), and congealed ox blood (seonji).
As these basic ingredients suggest, haejangguk originated in the alleyways near the palace, where beef — a precious ingredient — was available. While the king and court officials traveled along the main boulevards, workers and merchants passed through the side streets and alleys. There, vendors used the relatively cheap, leftover beef offal and blood to create an accessible, nutritious meal for these laborers. That’s why it’s located in Cheongjin-dong, in the alley right next to Jongno’s main road, and why it uses beef byproducts and affordable, easily available vegetables.

## Haejangguk in History
In the past, Korea had a curfew system — no one could be on the streets from midnight until 4 a.m. At 4 a.m. on the dot, people would flock to these Cheongjin-dong haejangguk restaurants to settle their stomachs. After the curfew was abolished, the restaurants became even more packed — customers who’d been drinking all night, customers who’d have a drink after eating haejangguk — there was barely room to stand, I heard. That’s why, until the COVID pandemic, many haejangguk restaurants in Korea operated 24 hours.

As you can tell from the ingredients, this type of haejangguk is best when made in large batches and simmered for a long time. If you ever get a chance to peek into Cheongjinok’s fourth-floor kitchen, you’ll see two enormous cauldrons — big enough to swallow the sun — bubbling away side by side. The broth is made by simmering beef offal, beef leg bones, and brisket for hours, then adding seonji and other vegetables to create a spicy haejangguk that pairs perfectly with soju.
If you were to name a traditional food for common people, a quintessentially Seoul dish for ordinary folks, haejangguk would certainly make the list. According to records, the first delivery food in the Joseon Dynasty was also a predecessor of this traditional haejangguk — _hyojong-gaeng_ was delivered to wealthy homes for hangover relief.

### Haejangguk, Up Close
One room, two clocks. Nobody finds it strange. The aristocrat's cotton-wrapped jar and the porter's dockside bowl turn out to be the same idea, a century and more apart: somebody keeps a pot on, and it feeds the end of one day and the start of the next out of the same ladle. So the worst hour of your day, whichever way you are traveling through it, has somewhere to go.

### On the Plate Today
It comes to you still boiling, in a stone bowl or a battered brass one, the surface trembling. Let it sit a moment. The steam is soybean paste first, then something deeper and beefy underneath, and a raw green note from the scallion dropped on top. Take a spoonful of just the broth, before the rice, off a clean spoon — the way you would taste anything worth tasting plain before you dress it. It is savory and round and a little earthy, salt and ferment before anything else, and this is where you understand it was never really about the meat.
Then you build it. Tip in the rice, or lift the small bowl of it waiting beside you and slide it under the surface; stir once so the grains loosen and the broth turns cloudy. Fish for the soft cabbage and the sprouts, still with a faint squeak to them. If there is seonji, take a piece — it gives way like the softest tofu, mineral and quiet, nothing like what you braced for. You add a spoon of salted shrimp or a pinch of chili if the counter has left them out, adjusting the bowl to the morning you are actually having.
Halfway down, something eases. Not your head, exactly, that takes longer, but the low animal panic of a bad start to the day, quietly switched off.
By the bottom you are warm to the fingertips, the rice gone soft, the bowl scraped. You say it without meaning to, the word for a heat that cools you from the inside. Siwonhada. Then you pay, and you go do the thing you woke up dreading, a little more able to face it than you were ten minutes before.

### In Your Kitchen
The Seoul blood-and-bone version is a project best left to the shops, but the gentler cousins are genuinely weeknight food, and they run on the same soybean-paste logic. The easiest place to start is bugeo-guk, dried-pollock soup. Soak a handful of dried pollock strips until soft, then turn them in a little sesame oil in the pot before you add any water — that quick fry is the whole secret, the step that turns a thin broth savory. Simmer fifteen minutes, loosen a heaping tablespoon of doenjang into it, and finish with beaten egg pulled through in ribbons and a lot of scallion. For a Jeonju-style morning instead, pour a clear anchovy-and-kelp broth over soybean sprouts and rice and simmer just until the sprouts lose their rawness — no more than five minutes, or they turn to straw — then top with a spoon of chili and toasted seaweed.
Either way the doenjang is the flavor here, not a background note, so it is worth using a properly fermented one with real depth rather than a flat, mass-market paste. What you keep on the shelf matters more than technique with a soup this plain.
These soups do not store like a red stew — they are morning food, best made in the amount you will eat, though a batch of the broth base keeps a couple of days covered. You will also find haejangguk has quietly gone twenty-four-hour and citywide, sold from all-night chains and, inevitably, as an instant pouch to microwave at 3 a.m. But the ones I trust keep older hours — open from before dawn until early afternoon and then done for the day, because this was always working people's food, made for the start of a shift and not the middle of one. Those late-night pouches have their place. The bowl worth knowing is still the one someone kept simmering while you slept.

### The Morning After, Taken Care Of
Call it hangover soup if you like — the word will do, the way most translations do, by getting the shape right and the soul wrong. Haejangguk is not a cure you take. It is a place you go when the night has run too long or the day starts too early, and someone has already thought of you enough to have the pot hot. That is the whole tradition, from a minister's warm delivery jar in 1925 to a market cauldron that has not been switched off since 1937: the quiet infrastructure of being looked after at the hour you least deserve it and most need it.
The next bowl you meet will be different from the last — clearer, redder, milder, regional in a dozen ways. Sit down anyway. Let it start your day for you.
* * *

### FAQ
**What does haejangguk taste like?**
Haejangguk tastes deeply savory and earthy, built on fermented soybean paste as much as on the meat that floats in it. The broth is round and salty with a faint ferment-bitterness from the doenjang, softened by long-cooked cabbage, radish, and soybean sprouts. Depending on the region it can be clear and gentle, milky and mild, or dark and spicy. What every version shares is a warming, restorative depth meant to be eaten with rice, first thing, when you need something steadying.
**What does "haejang" actually mean — is it about intestines?**
Haejang comes from an older word, haejeong, meaning to loosen or undo the aftereffects of drinking; guk simply means soup. Many people assume the jang refers to intestines, since so many haejangguk are full of them, but that is a coincidence of sound, not meaning. The name is really about the morning after — the ordeal of it, and the bowl that carries you through. It has nothing to do with any organ.
**Do you have to be hungover to eat haejangguk?**
Haejangguk is eaten by plenty of people who were never drunk the night before. It works as a warm, restorative breakfast for night-shift workers, early risers, and anyone facing a hard morning, hangover or not. Koreans treat it less as a remedy than as a ritual of starting the day with something hot and nourishing. The English name "hangover soup" is catchy, but it only tells part of the story.
**What's the difference between the regional types of haejangguk?**
Haejangguk is really a whole family of soups, each region answering the same need with what it has. Seoul's classic is a soybean-paste broth with cabbage, sprouts, and often seonji, gently set ox blood; Jeonju is known for a clear soybean-sprout soup poured over rice; coastal areas make a delicate freshwater-clam version, and many homes make a mild dried-pollock one. They range from soothing to fiery. Choosing among them is less about quality than about which morning you are having.
**Can I make haejangguk at home without special equipment?**

### FAQ
Haejangguk is very achievable at home if you begin with the gentler versions rather than the long-simmered blood-and-bone one. A dried-pollock soup (bugeo-guk) or a Jeonju-style soybean-sprout soup needs only a good doenjang or an anchovy-kelp broth, some sprouts or dried fish, an egg, and scallion. The single most important thing is the soybean paste, so use one with real fermented depth. Most of it comes together in under half an hour.
**Is there anything in American food like haejangguk?**
The closest American parallel is the classic hangover breakfast — the diner plate of eggs, hash, and bottomless coffee eaten to reset a rough morning. Both cultures reach for something warm, salty, and restorative the day after a long night. The difference is that haejangguk is soup, built on fermented soybean paste and eaten with rice, and that Koreans turned it into a whole regional tradition rather than a single greasy plate. If you have ever felt genuinely repaired by a breakfast, you already understand it.

If you ever get a chance to peek into Cheongjinok’s fourth-floor kitchen, you’ll see two enormous cauldrons — big enough to swallow the sun — bubbling away side by side. The broth is made by simmering beef offal, beef leg bones, and brisket for hours, then adding seonji and other vegetables to create a spicy haejangguk that pairs perfectly with soju.
If you were to name a traditional food for common people, a quintessentially Seoul dish for ordinary folks, haejangguk would certainly make the list. According to records, the first delivery food in the Joseon Dynasty was also a predecessor of this traditional haejangguk — _hyojong-gaeng_ was delivered to wealthy homes for hangover relief.

## The Irony of Korea’s Hangover Cure: It Makes You Want More Drinks
9 min read
Nov 21, 2025
Press enter or click to view image in full size
A Bloody Mary with pomegranate juice. The best thing in my life. | Photo by author. No reuse without permission
texts.2:
## The Most Dangerous Bloody Mary I Ever Had
One autumn evening, I attended a whisky tasting class in my role as a food editor. It was a unique session where a vegetable sommelier and whisky ambassador taught us how to pair vegetables and fruits with whisky. And there, as an aperitif, I encountered the most delicious Bloody Mary I’d ever tasted.
I never liked the raw, vegetal taste of tomato juice in cocktails, so I was shocked — how could this drink taste so much like a tomato, and yet so much like a fruit at the same time? When I asked the bartender, who had clearly put thought into crafting vegetable-based cocktails for this occasion, the secret turned out to be pomegranate juice.
Ah, so that was it! The rich, sweet pomegranate juice wrapped around the tomato’s vegetable-ness, bringing out its fruit-like qualities. Anyone drinking this would probably settle the “is tomato a fruit or vegetable?” debate firmly on the fruit side. Lost in this thought, I happily gulped down two glasses of this pomegranate Bloody Mary, and only when my vision started to swim did I realize: this Bloody Mary contained a generous amount of Glenfiddich whisky — the star of the tasting class.
Wait, wasn’t the Bloody Mary supposed to be a hangover-**cure** cocktail? What if I get drunk from drinking it? Oh, right — a hangover cure _cocktail_.
Imagine that: getting drunk from a drink meant to cure the effects of drinking. But I’m actually quite familiar with this ironic concept. We have it in Korea, too. Food meant for hangover recovery that actually calls for more drinking. Food that makes you suspect it became a hangover cure simply because drinkers loved it. Food that literally has “hangover cure” in its name: haejangguk (해장국).
Press enter or click to view image in full size
Cheongjinok’s Haejangguk. Eat it with the chili seasoning on the side mixed in. | Photo by author. No reuse without permission
texts.3:
## Literally “Korean Hangover Cure Soup”
Haejangguk. _Haejang_ means “hangover cure” in Korean, and _guk_ means “soup.” So the name itself literally means “soup for curing hangovers.”
Koreans have always loved soup-based dishes. In fact, there’s even a disparaging phrase for a high-maintenance husband — “someone who can’t eat rice without soup.” Rice with soup, a few side dishes, and kimchi — that’s the basic structure of a Korean meal.
So on those miserable mornings when the good feelings from last night’s drinking have evaporated and all that’s left is a churning stomach, turning to a hot soup dish for comfort — like chicken soup for the soul — is perhaps the most naturally Korean response.
Visit a restaurant famous for haejangguk in the morning. You’ll see middle-aged men whose faces clearly show last night’s drinking, pouring rice into their bubbling earthenware bowls of haejangguk and sweating profusely as they eat, exclaiming, “This is the stuff!” It’s like taking a sauna while eating. Then, once their stomachs settle a bit and the spicy broth lifts their spirits, there’s always someone who orders alcohol as a side drink.
Sir! If you want to detox from the alcohol, you shouldn’t be drinking more!
But it can’t be helped. Drinkers eat a lot of haejangguk because it’s the flavor profile drinkers love, and naturally, foods that drinkers love call for more drinking. At this point, you start to wonder if it’s even ironic that haejangguk leads to more drinking.
Press enter or click to view image in full size
Boiling pots of haejangguk side by side | Photo by author. No reuse without permission
texts.4:
## Understanding Korean Spicy Hangovers as You Age
When I first reached the legal drinking age and was busy testing my limits, I couldn’t understand these men eating haejangguk first thing in the morning. My stomach was churning, everything felt like it would come back up, and yet they were eating such heavy food? My hangover cure back then was usually fresh tomato juice — not from a can, but actually blended from real tomatoes. Or I’d try pizza or hamburgers, having heard that’s what college students overseas did.
But after two decades of drinking, I finally understand the men who order haejangguk the next morning. You have to have a slightly damaged stomach to appreciate it. Most modern Koreans — stressed, caffeinated, and overworked — have fragile stomachs. After a night of drinking, your once gentle pink stomach feels shredded. And like an itch on rough skin, only a good scratch brings relief — that scratch, for Koreans, is the fiery, spicy heat of haejangguk. It burns, it soothes, and somehow it heals.
Press enter or click to view image in full size
Sliced beef offal and soybean sprouts generously added to haejangguk | Photo by author. No reuse without permission
texts.5:
## The Haejangguk Street of Seoul
If you want to experience the most Korean-style hangover cure, head to Cheongjin-dong in downtown Seoul — a street that used to be filled with haejangguk restaurants. One of its most famous restaurants, _Cheongjinok_, dates back to 1937, when a grandmother first set up a cauldron on the street to sell soup to early risers. The third generation still runs it today.
Haejangguk is an old dish with a long and layered history. Sometimes the term is used loosely to describe any hot soup eaten to ease a hangover, but in its original form, haejangguk refers to a hearty beef-broth soup made with beef offal, chili flakes, dried radish greens (ugeoji), soybean sprouts (kongnamul), and congealed ox blood (seonji).
As these basic ingredients suggest, haejangguk originated in the alleyways near the palace, where beef — a precious ingredient — was available. While the king and court officials traveled along the main boulevards, workers and merchants passed through the side streets and alleys. There, vendors used the relatively cheap, leftover beef offal and blood to create an accessible, nutritious meal for these laborers. That’s why it’s located in Cheongjin-dong, in the alley right next to Jongno’s main road, and why it uses beef byproducts and affordable, easily available vegetables.
Press enter or click to view image in full size
Cheongjinok’s massive cauldron of haejangguk with seonji and napa cabbage | Photo by author. No reuse without permission
texts.6:
## Haejangguk in History
In the past, Korea had a curfew system — no one could be on the streets from midnight until 4 a.m. At 4 a.m. on the dot, people would flock to these Cheongjin-dong haejangguk restaurants to settle their stomachs. After the curfew was abolished, the restaurants became even more packed — customers who’d been drinking all night, customers who’d have a drink after eating haejangguk — there was barely room to stand, I heard. That’s why, until the COVID pandemic, many haejangguk restaurants in Korea operated 24 hours.
texts.7:

Join Medium for free to get updates from this writer.
Remember me for faster sign in
As you can tell from the ingredients, this type of haejangguk is best when made in large batches and simmered for a long time. If you ever get a chance to peek into Cheongjinok’s fourth-floor kitchen, you’ll see two enormous cauldrons — big enough to swallow the sun — bubbling away side by side. The broth is made by simmering beef offal, beef leg bones, and brisket for hours, then adding seonji and other vegetables to create a spicy haejangguk that pairs perfectly with soju.
If you were to name a traditional food for common people, a quintessentially Seoul dish for ordinary folks, haejangguk would certainly make the list. According to records, the first delivery food in the Joseon Dynasty was also a predecessor of this traditional haejangguk — _hyojong-gaeng_ was delivered to wealthy homes for hangover relief.
Press enter or click to view image in full size
Soybean Sprout Gukbap (“soup with rice”) at Hyundaiok in Jeonju, Korea | Photo by author. No reuse without permission

texts.4:
### Haejangguk, Up Close
One room, two clocks. Nobody finds it strange. The aristocrat's cotton-wrapped jar and the porter's dockside bowl turn out to be the same idea, a century and more apart: somebody keeps a pot on, and it feeds the end of one day and the start of the next out of the same ladle. So the worst hour of your day, whichever way you are traveling through it, has somewhere to go.
texts.5:
### On the Plate Today
It comes to you still boiling, in a stone bowl or a battered brass one, the surface trembling. Let it sit a moment. The steam is soybean paste first, then something deeper and beefy underneath, and a raw green note from the scallion dropped on top. Take a spoonful of just the broth, before the rice, off a clean spoon — the way you would taste anything worth tasting plain before you dress it. It is savory and round and a little earthy, salt and ferment before anything else, and this is where you understand it was never really about the meat.
Then you build it. Tip in the rice, or lift the small bowl of it waiting beside you and slide it under the surface; stir once so the grains loosen and the broth turns cloudy. Fish for the soft cabbage and the sprouts, still with a faint squeak to them. If there is seonji, take a piece — it gives way like the softest tofu, mineral and quiet, nothing like what you braced for. You add a spoon of salted shrimp or a pinch of chili if the counter has left them out, adjusting the bowl to the morning you are actually having.
Halfway down, something eases. Not your head, exactly, that takes longer, but the low animal panic of a bad start to the day, quietly switched off.
By the bottom you are warm to the fingertips, the rice gone soft, the bowl scraped. You say it without meaning to, the word for a heat that cools you from the inside. Siwonhada. Then you pay, and you go do the thing you woke up dreading, a little more able to face it than you were ten minutes before.
texts.6:
### In Your Kitchen
The Seoul blood-and-bone version is a project best left to the shops, but the gentler cousins are genuinely weeknight food, and they run on the same soybean-paste logic. The easiest place to start is bugeo-guk, dried-pollock soup. Soak a handful of dried pollock strips until soft, then turn them in a little sesame oil in the pot before you add any water — that quick fry is the whole secret, the step that turns a thin broth savory. Simmer fifteen minutes, loosen a heaping tablespoon of doenjang into it, and finish with beaten egg pulled through in ribbons and a lot of scallion. For a Jeonju-style morning instead, pour a clear anchovy-and-kelp broth over soybean sprouts and rice and simmer just until the sprouts lose their rawness — no more than five minutes, or they turn to straw — then top with a spoon of chili and toasted seaweed.
Either way the doenjang is the flavor here, not a background note, so it is worth using a properly fermented one with real depth rather than a flat, mass-market paste. What you keep on the shelf matters more than technique with a soup this plain.
These soups do not store like a red stew — they are morning food, best made in the amount you will eat, though a batch of the broth base keeps a couple of days covered. You will also find haejangguk has quietly gone twenty-four-hour and citywide, sold from all-night chains and, inevitably, as an instant pouch to microwave at 3 a.m. But the ones I trust keep older hours — open from before dawn until early afternoon and then done for the day, because this was always working people's food, made for the start of a shift and not the middle of one. Those late-night pouches have their place. The bowl worth knowing is still the one someone kept simmering while you slept.
texts.7:
### The Morning After, Taken Care Of
Call it hangover soup if you like — the word will do, the way most translations do, by getting the shape right and the soul wrong. Haejangguk is not a cure you take. It is a place you go when the night has run too long or the day starts too early, and someone has already thought of you enough to have the pot hot. That is the whole tradition, from a minister's warm delivery jar in 1925 to a market cauldron that has not been switched off since 1937: the quiet infrastructure of being looked after at the hour you least deserve it and most need it.
The next bowl you meet will be different from the last — clearer, redder, milder, regional in a dozen ways. Sit down anyway. Let it start your day for you.
* * *
texts.8:
### FAQ
**What does haejangguk taste like?**
Haejangguk tastes deeply savory and earthy, built on fermented soybean paste as much as on the meat that floats in it. The broth is round and salty with a faint ferment-bitterness from the doenjang, softened by long-cooked cabbage, radish, and soybean sprouts. Depending on the region it can be clear and gentle, milky and mild, or dark and spicy. What every version shares is a warming, restorative depth meant to be eaten with rice, first thing, when you need something steadying.
**What does "haejang" actually mean — is it about intestines?**
Haejang comes from an older word, haejeong, meaning to loosen or undo the aftereffects of drinking; guk simply means soup. Many people assume the jang refers to intestines, since so many haejangguk are full of them, but that is a coincidence of sound, not meaning. The name is really about the morning after — the ordeal of it, and the bowl that carries you through. It has nothing to do with any organ.
**Do you have to be hungover to eat haejangguk?**
Haejangguk is eaten by plenty of people who were never drunk the night before. It works as a warm, restorative breakfast for night-shift workers, early risers, and anyone facing a hard morning, hangover or not. Koreans treat it less as a remedy than as a ritual of starting the day with something hot and nourishing. The English name "hangover soup" is catchy, but it only tells part of the story.
**What's the difference between the regional types of haejangguk?**
Haejangguk is really a whole family of soups, each region answering the same need with what it has. Seoul's classic is a soybean-paste broth with cabbage, sprouts, and often seonji, gently set ox blood; Jeonju is known for a clear soybean-sprout soup poured over rice; coastal areas make a delicate freshwater-clam version, and many homes make a mild dried-pollock one. They range from soothing to fiery. Choosing among them is less about quality than about which morning you are having.
**Can I make haejangguk at home without special equipment?**
texts.9:
### FAQ
Haejangguk is very achievable at home if you begin with the gentler versions rather than the long-simmered blood-and-bone one. A dried-pollock soup (bugeo-guk) or a Jeonju-style soybean-sprout soup needs only a good doenjang or an anchovy-kelp broth, some sprouts or dried fish, an egg, and scallion. The single most important thing is the soybean paste, so use one with real fermented depth. Most of it comes together in under half an hour.
**Is there anything in American food like haejangguk?**
The closest American parallel is the classic hangover breakfast — the diner plate of eggs, hash, and bottomless coffee eaten to reset a rough morning. Both cultures reach for something warm, salty, and restorative the day after a long night. The difference is that haejangguk is soup, built on fermented soybean paste and eaten with rice, and that Koreans turned it into a whole regional tradition rather than a single greasy plate. If you have ever felt genuinely repaired by a breakfast, you already understand it.

Rustic meat and offal soup evolves at Jungang Haejang
It would be an understatement to say that Korean food is heavily based on soups and stews. Soup is a great way to stretch a meal so many could be fed cost consciously and to also make the most of modest ingredients and parts of meats that may not translate well into other dishes. In the food world today, what was considered food for “commoners” is now celebrated by an industry that has somehow taken a while to glorify the cheaper less desirable dishes already enjoyed and known by many.
Korean food beyond Korea is a more mainstream version of the classic dishes. Domestically, however, the authentic versions may sometimes be unrecognizable, as with the dish haejangguk, a robust soup with ingredients ranging from blood pudding to the simple bean sprout, and varied in style to test the limits of one’s appetite. Known for it’s heavy drinking culture, hangover cures have become mythical in Korea. Haejangguk is a culinary remedy, but today it can be enjoyed at any time for its warming and hearty savory flavor that fills and soothes the body and soul.

In Korea it is hard to find a restaurant that can balance a clean and relaxing ambience, pleasant service, and authentic Korean food. Koreans often eat their Korean food at home and only venture out for specialties better enjoyed by those who can deliver with an expertise.
At Jungang Haejangguk in Daechi-dong it is where you will find exactly that. In a modern space with a flavorful hanwoo version of haejangguk, as well as other classic meat dishes, Jungang Haejangguk is en pointe in bringing together a comfortable dining experience.
Owned by a family with a background in the meat business for over 30 years, and a patriarch who has passionately perfected his own haejangguk recipe for decades at home, Jungang’s rendition is all that you want from this meat laden soup filled to the rim with high quality ingredients such as cow stomach and seonji, also known as blood pudding, the mandatory siraegi, reconstituted radish greens, and a deep refreshing broth made from ox bones and other beef cuts simmered for 5 hours no less. Jungang Haejangguk can be appreciated by those who want fine quality meat dishes, as it exceeds through its superior ingredients and lovingly made high standard.

## The Irony of Korea’s Hangover Cure: It Makes You Want More Drinks
9 min read
Nov 21, 2025
Press enter or click to view image in full size
A Bloody Mary with pomegranate juice. The best thing in my life. | Photo by author. No reuse without permission

## The Most Dangerous Bloody Mary I Ever Had
One autumn evening, I attended a whisky tasting class in my role as a food editor. It was a unique session where a vegetable sommelier and whisky ambassador taught us how to pair vegetables and fruits with whisky. And there, as an aperitif, I encountered the most delicious Bloody Mary I’d ever tasted.
I never liked the raw, vegetal taste of tomato juice in cocktails, so I was shocked — how could this drink taste so much like a tomato, and yet so much like a fruit at the same time? When I asked the bartender, who had clearly put thought into crafting vegetable-based cocktails for this occasion, the secret turned out to be pomegranate juice.
Ah, so that was it! The rich, sweet pomegranate juice wrapped around the tomato’s vegetable-ness, bringing out its fruit-like qualities. Anyone drinking this would probably settle the “is tomato a fruit or vegetable?” debate firmly on the fruit side. Lost in this thought, I happily gulped down two glasses of this pomegranate Bloody Mary, and only when my vision started to swim did I realize: this Bloody Mary contained a generous amount of Glenfiddich whisky — the star of the tasting class.
Wait, wasn’t the Bloody Mary supposed to be a hangover-**cure** cocktail? What if I get drunk from drinking it? Oh, right — a hangover cure _cocktail_.
Imagine that: getting drunk from a drink meant to cure the effects of drinking. But I’m actually quite familiar with this ironic concept. We have it in Korea, too. Food meant for hangover recovery that actually calls for more drinking. Food that makes you suspect it became a hangover cure simply because drinkers loved it. Food that literally has “hangover cure” in its name: haejangguk (해장국).
Press enter or click to view image in full size
Cheongjinok’s Haejangguk. Eat it with the chili seasoning on the side mixed in. | Photo by author. No reuse without permission

## Literally “Korean Hangover Cure Soup”
Haejangguk. _Haejang_ means “hangover cure” in Korean, and _guk_ means “soup.” So the name itself literally means “soup for curing hangovers.”
Koreans have always loved soup-based dishes. In fact, there’s even a disparaging phrase for a high-maintenance husband — “someone who can’t eat rice without soup.” Rice with soup, a few side dishes, and kimchi — that’s the basic structure of a Korean meal.
So on those miserable mornings when the good feelings from last night’s drinking have evaporated and all that’s left is a churning stomach, turning to a hot soup dish for comfort — like chicken soup for the soul — is perhaps the most naturally Korean response.
Visit a restaurant famous for haejangguk in the morning. You’ll see middle-aged men whose faces clearly show last night’s drinking, pouring rice into their bubbling earthenware bowls of haejangguk and sweating profusely as they eat, exclaiming, “This is the stuff!” It’s like taking a sauna while eating. Then, once their stomachs settle a bit and the spicy broth lifts their spirits, there’s always someone who orders alcohol as a side drink.
Sir! If you want to detox from the alcohol, you shouldn’t be drinking more!
But it can’t be helped. Drinkers eat a lot of haejangguk because it’s the flavor profile drinkers love, and naturally, foods that drinkers love call for more drinking. At this point, you start to wonder if it’s even ironic that haejangguk leads to more drinking.
Press enter or click to view image in full size
Boiling pots of haejangguk side by side | Photo by author. No reuse without permission

## Understanding Korean Spicy Hangovers as You Age
When I first reached the legal drinking age and was busy testing my limits, I couldn’t understand these men eating haejangguk first thing in the morning. My stomach was churning, everything felt like it would come back up, and yet they were eating such heavy food? My hangover cure back then was usually fresh tomato juice — not from a can, but actually blended from real tomatoes. Or I’d try pizza or hamburgers, having heard that’s what college students overseas did.
But after two decades of drinking, I finally understand the men who order haejangguk the next morning. You have to have a slightly damaged stomach to appreciate it. Most modern Koreans — stressed, caffeinated, and overworked — have fragile stomachs. After a night of drinking, your once gentle pink stomach feels shredded. And like an itch on rough skin, only a good scratch brings relief — that scratch, for Koreans, is the fiery, spicy heat of haejangguk. It burns, it soothes, and somehow it heals.
Press enter or click to view image in full size
Sliced beef offal and soybean sprouts generously added to haejangguk | Photo by author. No reuse without permission

## The Haejangguk Street of Seoul
If you want to experience the most Korean-style hangover cure, head to Cheongjin-dong in downtown Seoul — a street that used to be filled with haejangguk restaurants. One of its most famous restaurants, _Cheongjinok_, dates back to 1937, when a grandmother first set up a cauldron on the street to sell soup to early risers. The third generation still runs it today.
Haejangguk is an old dish with a long and layered history. Sometimes the term is used loosely to describe any hot soup eaten to ease a hangover, but in its original form, haejangguk refers to a hearty beef-broth soup made with beef offal, chili flakes, dried radish greens (ugeoji), soybean sprouts (kongnamul), and congealed ox blood (seonji).
As these basic ingredients suggest, haejangguk originated in the alleyways near the palace, where beef — a precious ingredient — was available. While the king and court officials traveled along the main boulevards, workers and merchants passed through the side streets and alleys. There, vendors used the relatively cheap, leftover beef offal and blood to create an accessible, nutritious meal for these laborers. That’s why it’s located in Cheongjin-dong, in the alley right next to Jongno’s main road, and why it uses beef byproducts and affordable, easily available vegetables.
Press enter or click to view image in full size
Cheongjinok’s massive cauldron of haejangguk with seonji and napa cabbage | Photo by author. No reuse without permission

## Haejangguk in History
In the past, Korea had a curfew system — no one could be on the streets from midnight until 4 a.m. At 4 a.m. on the dot, people would flock to these Cheongjin-dong haejangguk restaurants to settle their stomachs. After the curfew was abolished, the restaurants became even more packed — customers who’d been drinking all night, customers who’d have a drink after eating haejangguk — there was barely room to stand, I heard. That’s why, until the COVID pandemic, many haejangguk restaurants in Korea operated 24 hours.

## Get Yeonjoo Jung’s stories in your inbox
Join Medium for free to get updates from this writer.
Remember me for faster sign in
As you can tell from the ingredients, this type of haejangguk is best when made in large batches and simmered for a long time. If you ever get a chance to peek into Cheongjinok’s fourth-floor kitchen, you’ll see two enormous cauldrons — big enough to swallow the sun — bubbling away side by side. The broth is made by simmering beef offal, beef leg bones, and brisket for hours, then adding seonji and other vegetables to create a spicy haejangguk that pairs perfectly with soju.
If you were to name a traditional food for common people, a quintessentially Seoul dish for ordinary folks, haejangguk would certainly make the list. According to records, the first delivery food in the Joseon Dynasty was also a predecessor of this traditional haejangguk — _hyojong-gaeng_ was delivered to wealthy homes for hangover relief.

Chunks: 4,5,6,7,8,9
### Haejangguk, Up Close
One room, two clocks. Nobody finds it strange. The aristocrat's cotton-wrapped jar and the porter's dockside bowl turn out to be the same idea, a century and more apart: somebody keeps a pot on, and it feeds the end of one day and the start of the next out of the same ladle. So the worst hour of your day, whichever way you are traveling through it, has somewhere to go.

### On the Plate Today
It comes to you still boiling, in a stone bowl or a battered brass one, the surface trembling. Let it sit a moment. The steam is soybean paste first, then something deeper and beefy underneath, and a raw green note from the scallion dropped on top. Take a spoonful of just the broth, before the rice, off a clean spoon — the way you would taste anything worth tasting plain before you dress it. It is savory and round and a little earthy, salt and ferment before anything else, and this is where you understand it was never really about the meat.
Then you build it. Tip in the rice, or lift the small bowl of it waiting beside you and slide it under the surface; stir once so the grains loosen and the broth turns cloudy. Fish for the soft cabbage and the sprouts, still with a faint squeak to them. If there is seonji, take a piece — it gives way like the softest tofu, mineral and quiet, nothing like what you braced for. You add a spoon of salted shrimp or a pinch of chili if the counter has left them out, adjusting the bowl to the morning you are actually having.
Halfway down, something eases. Not your head, exactly, that takes longer, but the low animal panic of a bad start to the day, quietly switched off.
By the bottom you are warm to the fingertips, the rice gone soft, the bowl scraped. You say it without meaning to, the word for a heat that cools you from the inside. Siwonhada. Then you pay, and you go do the thing you woke up dreading, a little more able to face it than you were ten minutes before.

### In Your Kitchen
The Seoul blood-and-bone version is a project best left to the shops, but the gentler cousins are genuinely weeknight food, and they run on the same soybean-paste logic. The easiest place to start is bugeo-guk, dried-pollock soup. Soak a handful of dried pollock strips until soft, then turn them in a little sesame oil in the pot before you add any water — that quick fry is the whole secret, the step that turns a thin broth savory. Simmer fifteen minutes, loosen a heaping tablespoon of doenjang into it, and finish with beaten egg pulled through in ribbons and a lot of scallion. For a Jeonju-style morning instead, pour a clear anchovy-and-kelp broth over soybean sprouts and rice and simmer just until the sprouts lose their rawness — no more than five minutes, or they turn to straw — then top with a spoon of chili and toasted seaweed.
Either way the doenjang is the flavor here, not a background note, so it is worth using a properly fermented one with real depth rather than a flat, mass-market paste. What you keep on the shelf matters more than technique with a soup this plain.
These soups do not store like a red stew — they are morning food, best made in the amount you will eat, though a batch of the broth base keeps a couple of days covered. You will also find haejangguk has quietly gone twenty-four-hour and citywide, sold from all-night chains and, inevitably, as an instant pouch to microwave at 3 a.m. But the ones I trust keep older hours — open from before dawn until early afternoon and then done for the day, because this was always working people's food, made for the start of a shift and not the middle of one. Those late-night pouches have their place. The bowl worth knowing is still the one someone kept simmering while you slept.

### The Morning After, Taken Care Of
Call it hangover soup if you like — the word will do, the way most translations do, by getting the shape right and the soul wrong. Haejangguk is not a cure you take. It is a place you go when the night has run too long or the day starts too early, and someone has already thought of you enough to have the pot hot. That is the whole tradition, from a minister's warm delivery jar in 1925 to a market cauldron that has not been switched off since 1937: the quiet infrastructure of being looked after at the hour you least deserve it and most need it.
The next bowl you meet will be different from the last — clearer, redder, milder, regional in a dozen ways. Sit down anyway. Let it start your day for you.
* * *

### FAQ
**What does haejangguk taste like?**
Haejangguk tastes deeply savory and earthy, built on fermented soybean paste as much as on the meat that floats in it. The broth is round and salty with a faint ferment-bitterness from the doenjang, softened by long-cooked cabbage, radish, and soybean sprouts. Depending on the region it can be clear and gentle, milky and mild, or dark and spicy. What every version shares is a warming, restorative depth meant to be eaten with rice, first thing, when you need something steadying.
**What does "haejang" actually mean — is it about intestines?**
Haejang comes from an older word, haejeong, meaning to loosen or undo the aftereffects of drinking; guk simply means soup. Many people assume the jang refers to intestines, since so many haejangguk are full of them, but that is a coincidence of sound, not meaning. The name is really about the morning after — the ordeal of it, and the bowl that carries you through. It has nothing to do with any organ.
**Do you have to be hungover to eat haejangguk?**
Haejangguk is eaten by plenty of people who were never drunk the night before. It works as a warm, restorative breakfast for night-shift workers, early risers, and anyone facing a hard morning, hangover or not. Koreans treat it less as a remedy than as a ritual of starting the day with something hot and nourishing. The English name "hangover soup" is catchy, but it only tells part of the story.
**What's the difference between the regional types of haejangguk?**
Haejangguk is really a whole family of soups, each region answering the same need with what it has. Seoul's classic is a soybean-paste broth with cabbage, sprouts, and often seonji, gently set ox blood; Jeonju is known for a clear soybean-sprout soup poured over rice; coastal areas make a delicate freshwater-clam version, and many homes make a mild dried-pollock one. They range from soothing to fiery. Choosing among them is less about quality than about which morning you are having.
**Can I make haejangguk at home without special equipment?**

### FAQ
Haejangguk is very achievable at home if you begin with the gentler versions rather than the long-simmered blood-and-bone one. A dried-pollock soup (bugeo-guk) or a Jeonju-style soybean-sprout soup needs only a good doenjang or an anchovy-kelp broth, some sprouts or dried fish, an egg, and scallion. The single most important thing is the soybean paste, so use one with real fermented depth. Most of it comes together in under half an hour.
**Is there anything in American food like haejangguk?**
The closest American parallel is the classic hangover breakfast — the diner plate of eggs, hash, and bottomless coffee eaten to reset a rough morning. Both cultures reach for something warm, salty, and restorative the day after a long night. The difference is that haejangguk is soup, built on fermented soybean paste and eaten with rice, and that Koreans turned it into a whole regional tradition rather than a single greasy plate. If you have ever felt genuinely repaired by a breakfast, you already understand it.

Title: Thrillable Hours: Erin Geiger Smith, Journalist and Author
Chunks: 0,1,2,3,4,5
_Welcome back to_ _Thrillable Hours, \_my interview series about alternative careers for lawyers.\__
_I met Erin through Anthony De Rosa, who was then the social media head honcho at Reuters. Now working for Circa, Anthony saw that we had both shifted from law to a broader but more satisfying (for us at least) path, and connected us._
_Erin was also at Reuters until recently and is now working as a freelance journalist while still based in New York.Her husband recently made his way to Saigon for work, so it was great to meet (and feed) her other half here too._
_Here are Erin’s thoughts on her career trajectory, answering the usual 5 Thrillable Hours questions._
* * *
Table of Contents

### What made you decide to leave private practice? Was there a particular moment that catalyzed the decision for you?
I was a journalism major in undergrad, and could just never get the idea of being a journalist out of my head. I left my Texas law firm in 2007 and moved to one in New York. While I’d had a prominent role in my cases in Texas, in New York I had way less responsibility and it felt like more of a grind. Being in New York,which is obviously the centre of the media industry in the USA, also made making the change seem more possible. I’d just turned 29 and it felt like “now or never”, so I applied to Columbia’s journalism school. I was to hear whether I got in or not on April 1. I quit the law firm the last Friday of March so that even if I didn’t get in, I’d have no choice but to somehow make a career in reporting work. Luckily I was admitted, as I don’t know where I’d be without the contacts I made at Columbia.
[![Image 2: Photo & Video Sharing by SmugMug](blob:http://localhost/e8a57f4972516a1d3218894eabc89576)](http://legalnomads.smugmug.com/Travel/Photos-for-Posts/n-Rd5X4/i-rRsPGtG/A "Photo & Video Sharing by SmugMug")

### What do you find most fulfilling about your current job?
I’ve always been a news junkie, so meeting and being friends with reporters I admire, as well as just playing a tiny part in providing people information (and sometimes getting that information first!) is still really exciting to me. I also like that I can write about whatever I want — from serious things like intellectual property law to fun things like fashion.I covered a Supreme Court IP case involving Nike, for instance, and got to talk to all of the high court advocates, as well as the “little guy” who originally brought the case. I also used my interest in lifestyle reporting to write a few fashion law articles a year, which turned into covering fashion shows and interviewing the author of a book on Balenciaga. None of it felt like work.
[![Image 3](blob:http://localhost/e8a57f4972516a1d3218894eabc89576)](http://legalnomads.smugmug.com/Travel/Photos-for-Posts/n-Rd5X4/i-9nSfbkg/A)

### Do you have any advice for professionals who are interested in branching out from traditional practice but concerned about what is out there?
If you’re not enjoying being a lawyer, set a date by which you no longer want to be one and stick to it. Also, think of a field you’d like to work in and people who are prominent in that field and call them and ask them how they got there and if they have any advice for you. When I was first learning to be a reporter, it was scary to call people, but it turns out most people like to talk,especially about themselves, and most people like to help other people. And even if 9 out of 10 people ignore your email, the info you get from the one who answers will be worth the effort.Obviously there are some limits to this — it’s unlikely you can achieve your dream of becoming a professional basketball player by calling Kevin Durant — but chances are your lawyer skills can transfer to something you would like to do.
Also, it’s at first hard to give up the idea that lawyering is an “important” job and that your new career might come with less prestige. First of all, so what? But second of all, if it’s important to you, it’s important. I know an associate at a top firm in New York who wants to leave to become a fitness instructor. I really, really hope she does it. She’d be so great, and so happy. I’ve also NEVER known a lawyer who left to do something else and was sorry they did. It doesn’t mean it’s easy — I’ve had plenty of bad days — but it’s always been worth it.
One caveat, though — if you’re a big firm lawyer, embrace that you’re probably going to make less money. Make a plan for that change in lifestyle. (Full disclosure: Going to Texas means that my law schools debt was totally manageable,and my husband has always been fully employed. So if my journalism career tanked, I wasn’t going to starve. But I don’t quite have the clothes budget I used to.)

### Do you still identify as a lawyer or use the skills you developed in your legal training?
I don’t really identify as a lawyer anymore, and don’t necessarily want to be identified as one. But since I’ve spent lots of time covering legal news, I’ve definitely used the legal training. That said, learning not to be a lawyer has been really important, too. Lawyers don’t like to ask questions they don’t know the answers to, which is a major liability for a journalist. I’m also still trying to not write like a lawyer. Sorry, lawyers … most of us are terrible writers.

### What do you have to say to those who tell me lawyers can’t have fun?
That’s like people who say women aren’t funny. I know lots of still-practicing lawyers who have fun at their jobs — a partner that actually goes to trial a lot, a deal lawyer for a major tech company, and a genius litigator who works for a state attorney general’s office, to name a few. But if you’re a lawyer who wants to do something else, I can almost guarantee you’ll have more fun if you take the leap.
**2020 Update:** Erin has just released her first book, published by Harper Collins. Entitled _Thank You for Voting: The Past, Present, and Future of Voting_, the book looks at the past, present, and future of voting. Erin examines long and continuing fight for voting equality, why so few Americans today vote, and innovative ways to educate and motivate them; included are checklists of what to do before election day to prepare to vote and encourage others. You can pick up the book here, with a review here from Publishers Weekly.
_* * *_
![Image 4: erin geiger smith](blob:http://localhost/37995246866d8e4474ec90d5ffad8b83)_Erin Geiger Smith grew up in tiny Liberty, Texas and went to college and law school at the University of Texas in Austin. She began her legal career at Andrews Kurth in Texas and finished it almost five years later at Chadbourne & Parke in New York. She received a masters degree from Columbia University’s Graduate School of Journalism and started Business Insider’s law blog before becoming a legal reporter at Reuters. She wrote on topics including major litigation and intellectual property while weaselling her way into things like reporting from New York Fashion Week and interviewing Molly Ringwald. She is now a freelance reporter in New York covering all of those topics and more for publications including Fashionista and The Wall Street Journal. Don’t follow her on Instagram if you’ll tire of pictures of Central Park, her chihuahua, or her 3 month old son, Reed. She tweets about law, lifestyle and everything in betweenhere._

**Mehdi Raza Hasan**[[a]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mehdi_Hasan#cite_note-1) (born 10 July 1979) is a British-American broadcaster, journalist, progressive political commentator, and founder of the media company Zeteo. He presented _The Mehdi Hasan Show_ on Peacock from October 2020 and on MSNBC from February 2021 until the show's cancellation in November 2023.

A graduate of Christ Church, Oxford, Hasan began his television career as a researcher and then producer on ITV's Jonathan Dimbleby programme. Following a stint on the BBC's _The Politics Show_, he became deputy executive producer on Sky's breakfast show _Sunrise_ before moving to Channel 4 as their editor of news and current affairs. In 2009, he was appointed senior editor for politics at the _New Statesman_. In 2012, he became a presenter on Al Jazeera English, and in 2015, he moved to Washington, D.C., to work full-time for Al Jazeera on _UpFront_ and host the _Deconstructed_ podcast produced by the online publication _The Intercept_ from 2018 to 2020.
Hasan is the author of _Win Every Argument_ and the co-author of a biography of former Labour Party leader Ed Miliband. He was formerly the political editor of the UK edition of _The Huffington Post_ and the presenter of the Al Jazeera English shows _The Café_, _Head to Head_, and _UpFront_. After departing MSNBC, Hasan joined _The Guardian_ as a columnist and created the digital media company Zeteo in February 2024, and returned as host of _Head to Head_ in June that year.

## Early life and education
Hasan was born on 10 July 1979[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mehdi_Hasan#cite_note-2)[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mehdi_Hasan#cite_note-3) in Swindon, Wiltshire, in South West England to Shia Muslim parents from Hyderabad in Telangana, Southern India.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mehdi_Hasan#cite_note-4)[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mehdi_Hasan#cite_note-tweet1-5)[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mehdi_Hasan#cite_note-6) His mother is a doctor and his father, an engineer. Hasan grew up in Harrow, an area of outer North West London.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mehdi_Hasan#cite_note-7)[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mehdi_Hasan#cite_note-:2-8)
Hasan was privately educated at [Merchant Taylors' School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Merchant_Taylors'_School,_Northwood "Merchant Taylors' School, Northwood"), an independent day school for boys at Sandy Lodge, in the Three Rivers District of Hertfordshire, near Northwood in North West London.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mehdi_Hasan#cite_note-mts-9) Hasan and British actor and rapper Riz Ahmed were classmates.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mehdi_Hasan#cite_note-:3-10) Hasan subsequently went up to Christ Church, University of Oxford, graduating in 2000 with a Bachelor of Arts (BA) degree in philosophy, politics and economics (PPE).[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mehdi_Hasan#cite_note-mts-9)

## Career
### 2009–2011: Early beginnings
Hasan worked as a researcher and then producer on ITV's _Jonathan Dimbleby_ programme,[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mehdi_Hasan#cite_note-telqt-11) with a brief period in between on BBC One's _The Politics Show_.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mehdi_Hasan#cite_note-telqt-11) Following this, he became deputy executive producer on Sky's breakfast show _Sunrise_,[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mehdi_Hasan#cite_note-telqt-11) before moving to Channel 4 as their editor of news and current affairs.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mehdi_Hasan#cite_note-pg-12) He was appointed senior editor for politics at the _New Statesman_ in late spring of 2009,[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mehdi_Hasan#cite_note-13) where he stayed until May 2012, then becoming political director of _The Huffington Post_ website.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mehdi_Hasan#cite_note-pg-12)[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mehdi_Hasan#cite_note-14)

## Career
### 2012–2020: _Al Jazeera_ and _The Intercept_
Hasan and Martin Kettle at a Labour Party conference in 2012
Hasan became a presenter on Al Jazeera's English news channel in May 2012.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mehdi_Hasan#cite_note-15) Hasan has appeared (six times) on the BBC's _Question Time_ programme,[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mehdi_Hasan#cite_note-16) and the Sunday morning programmes _The Big Questions_ and _Sunday Morning Live_.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mehdi_Hasan#cite_note-17)[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mehdi_Hasan#cite_note-18) On _Question Time_ in October 2013, Hasan called the _Daily Mail_ "immigrant-bashing, woman-hating, Muslim-smearing, NHS-undermining, [and] gay-baiting". The newspaper responded by printing an e-mail he had sent them in 2010, in which he asked for a column and praised several of their viewpoints. Hasan said the "sycophantic" letter was his writing but criticised the newspaper's decision to publish it.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mehdi_Hasan#cite_note-19)[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mehdi_Hasan#cite_note-20)

**Mehdi Raza Hasan**[[a]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mehdi_Hasan#cite_note-1) (born 10 July 1979) is a British-American broadcaster, journalist, progressive political commentator, and founder of the media company Zeteo. He presented _The Mehdi Hasan Show_ on Peacock from October 2020 and on MSNBC from February 2021 until the show's cancellation in November 2023.
texts.1:
A graduate of Christ Church, Oxford, Hasan began his television career as a researcher and then producer on ITV's Jonathan Dimbleby programme. Following a stint on the BBC's _The Politics Show_, he became deputy executive producer on Sky's breakfast show _Sunrise_ before moving to Channel 4 as their editor of news and current affairs. In 2009, he was appointed senior editor for politics at the _New Statesman_. In 2012, he became a presenter on Al Jazeera English, and in 2015, he moved to Washington, D.C., to work full-time for Al Jazeera on _UpFront_ and host the _Deconstructed_ podcast produced by the online publication _The Intercept_ from 2018 to 2020.
Hasan is the author of _Win Every Argument_ and the co-author of a biography of former Labour Party leader Ed Miliband. He was formerly the political editor of the UK edition of _The Huffington Post_ and the presenter of the Al Jazeera English shows _The Café_, _Head to Head_, and _UpFront_. After departing MSNBC, Hasan joined _The Guardian_ as a columnist and created the digital media company Zeteo in February 2024, and returned as host of _Head to Head_ in June that year.
texts.2:
## Early life and education
Hasan was born on 10 July 1979[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mehdi_Hasan#cite_note-2)[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mehdi_Hasan#cite_note-3) in Swindon, Wiltshire, in South West England to Shia Muslim parents from Hyderabad in Telangana, Southern India.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mehdi_Hasan#cite_note-4)[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mehdi_Hasan#cite_note-tweet1-5)[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mehdi_Hasan#cite_note-6) His mother is a doctor and his father, an engineer. Hasan grew up in Harrow, an area of outer North West London.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mehdi_Hasan#cite_note-7)[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mehdi_Hasan#cite_note-:2-8)
Hasan was privately educated at [Merchant Taylors' School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Merchant_Taylors'_School,_Northwood "Merchant Taylors' School, Northwood"), an independent day school for boys at Sandy Lodge, in the Three Rivers District of Hertfordshire, near Northwood in North West London.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mehdi_Hasan#cite_note-mts-9) Hasan and British actor and rapper Riz Ahmed were classmates.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mehdi_Hasan#cite_note-:3-10) Hasan subsequently went up to Christ Church, University of Oxford, graduating in 2000 with a Bachelor of Arts (BA) degree in philosophy, politics and economics (PPE).[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mehdi_Hasan#cite_note-mts-9)
texts.3:
## Career
### 2009–2011: Early beginnings
Hasan worked as a researcher and then producer on ITV's _Jonathan Dimbleby_ programme,[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mehdi_Hasan#cite_note-telqt-11) with a brief period in between on BBC One's _The Politics Show_.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mehdi_Hasan#cite_note-telqt-11) Following this, he became deputy executive producer on Sky's breakfast show _Sunrise_,[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mehdi_Hasan#cite_note-telqt-11) before moving to Channel 4 as their editor of news and current affairs.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mehdi_Hasan#cite_note-pg-12) He was appointed senior editor for politics at the _New Statesman_ in late spring of 2009,[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mehdi_Hasan#cite_note-13) where he stayed until May 2012, then becoming political director of _The Huffington Post_ website.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mehdi_Hasan#cite_note-pg-12)[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mehdi_Hasan#cite_note-14)
texts.4:
## Career
### 2012–2020: _Al Jazeera_ and _The Intercept_
Hasan and Martin Kettle at a Labour Party conference in 2012
Hasan became a presenter on Al Jazeera's English news channel in May 2012.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mehdi_Hasan#cite_note-15) Hasan has appeared (six times) on the BBC's _Question Time_ programme,[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mehdi_Hasan#cite_note-16) and the Sunday morning programmes _The Big Questions_ and _Sunday Morning Live_.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mehdi_Hasan#cite_note-17)[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mehdi_Hasan#cite_note-18) On _Question Time_ in October 2013, Hasan called the _Daily Mail_ "immigrant-bashing, woman-hating, Muslim-smearing, NHS-undermining, [and] gay-baiting". The newspaper responded by printing an e-mail he had sent them in 2010, in which he asked for a column and praised several of their viewpoints. Hasan said the "sycophantic" letter was his writing but criticised the newspaper's decision to publish it.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mehdi_Hasan#cite_note-19)[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mehdi_Hasan#cite_note-20)

_Welcome back to_ _Thrillable Hours, \_my interview series about alternative careers for lawyers.\__
_I met Erin through Anthony De Rosa, who was then the social media head honcho at Reuters. Now working for Circa, Anthony saw that we had both shifted from law to a broader but more satisfying (for us at least) path, and connected us._
_Erin was also at Reuters until recently and is now working as a freelance journalist while still based in New York.Her husband recently made his way to Saigon for work, so it was great to meet (and feed) her other half here too._
_Here are Erin’s thoughts on her career trajectory, answering the usual 5 Thrillable Hours questions._
* * *
Table of Contents
texts.1:
### What made you decide to leave private practice? Was there a particular moment that catalyzed the decision for you?
I was a journalism major in undergrad, and could just never get the idea of being a journalist out of my head. I left my Texas law firm in 2007 and moved to one in New York. While I’d had a prominent role in my cases in Texas, in New York I had way less responsibility and it felt like more of a grind. Being in New York,which is obviously the centre of the media industry in the USA, also made making the change seem more possible. I’d just turned 29 and it felt like “now or never”, so I applied to Columbia’s journalism school. I was to hear whether I got in or not on April 1. I quit the law firm the last Friday of March so that even if I didn’t get in, I’d have no choice but to somehow make a career in reporting work. Luckily I was admitted, as I don’t know where I’d be without the contacts I made at Columbia.
[![Image 2: Photo & Video Sharing by SmugMug](blob:http://localhost/e8a57f4972516a1d3218894eabc89576)](http://legalnomads.smugmug.com/Travel/Photos-for-Posts/n-Rd5X4/i-rRsPGtG/A "Photo & Video Sharing by SmugMug")
texts.2:
### What do you find most fulfilling about your current job?
I’ve always been a news junkie, so meeting and being friends with reporters I admire, as well as just playing a tiny part in providing people information (and sometimes getting that information first!) is still really exciting to me. I also like that I can write about whatever I want — from serious things like intellectual property law to fun things like fashion.I covered a Supreme Court IP case involving Nike, for instance, and got to talk to all of the high court advocates, as well as the “little guy” who originally brought the case. I also used my interest in lifestyle reporting to write a few fashion law articles a year, which turned into covering fashion shows and interviewing the author of a book on Balenciaga. None of it felt like work.
[![Image 3](blob:http://localhost/e8a57f4972516a1d3218894eabc89576)](http://legalnomads.smugmug.com/Travel/Photos-for-Posts/n-Rd5X4/i-9nSfbkg/A)
texts.3:
### Do you have any advice for professionals who are interested in branching out from traditional practice but concerned about what is out there?
If you’re not enjoying being a lawyer, set a date by which you no longer want to be one and stick to it. Also, think of a field you’d like to work in and people who are prominent in that field and call them and ask them how they got there and if they have any advice for you. When I was first learning to be a reporter, it was scary to call people, but it turns out most people like to talk,especially about themselves, and most people like to help other people. And even if 9 out of 10 people ignore your email, the info you get from the one who answers will be worth the effort.Obviously there are some limits to this — it’s unlikely you can achieve your dream of becoming a professional basketball player by calling Kevin Durant — but chances are your lawyer skills can transfer to something you would like to do.
Also, it’s at first hard to give up the idea that lawyering is an “important” job and that your new career might come with less prestige. First of all, so what? But second of all, if it’s important to you, it’s important. I know an associate at a top firm in New York who wants to leave to become a fitness instructor. I really, really hope she does it. She’d be so great, and so happy. I’ve also NEVER known a lawyer who left to do something else and was sorry they did. It doesn’t mean it’s easy — I’ve had plenty of bad days — but it’s always been worth it.
One caveat, though — if you’re a big firm lawyer, embrace that you’re probably going to make less money. Make a plan for that change in lifestyle. (Full disclosure: Going to Texas means that my law schools debt was totally manageable,and my husband has always been fully employed. So if my journalism career tanked, I wasn’t going to starve. But I don’t quite have the clothes budget I used to.)
texts.4:
### Do you still identify as a lawyer or use the skills you developed in your legal training?
I don’t really identify as a lawyer anymore, and don’t necessarily want to be identified as one. But since I’ve spent lots of time covering legal news, I’ve definitely used the legal training. That said, learning not to be a lawyer has been really important, too. Lawyers don’t like to ask questions they don’t know the answers to, which is a major liability for a journalist. I’m also still trying to not write like a lawyer. Sorry, lawyers … most of us are terrible writers.
texts.5:
### What do you have to say to those who tell me lawyers can’t have fun?
That’s like people who say women aren’t funny. I know lots of still-practicing lawyers who have fun at their jobs — a partner that actually goes to trial a lot, a deal lawyer for a major tech company, and a genius litigator who works for a state attorney general’s office, to name a few. But if you’re a lawyer who wants to do something else, I can almost guarantee you’ll have more fun if you take the leap.
**2020 Update:** Erin has just released her first book, published by Harper Collins. Entitled _Thank You for Voting: The Past, Present, and Future of Voting_, the book looks at the past, present, and future of voting. Erin examines long and continuing fight for voting equality, why so few Americans today vote, and innovative ways to educate and motivate them; included are checklists of what to do before election day to prepare to vote and encourage others. You can pick up the book here, with a review here from Publishers Weekly.
_* * *_
![Image 4: erin geiger smith](blob:http://localhost/37995246866d8e4474ec90d5ffad8b83)_Erin Geiger Smith grew up in tiny Liberty, Texas and went to college and law school at the University of Texas in Austin. She began her legal career at Andrews Kurth in Texas and finished it almost five years later at Chadbourne & Parke in New York. She received a masters degree from Columbia University’s Graduate School of Journalism and started Business Insider’s law blog before becoming a legal reporter at Reuters. She wrote on topics including major litigation and intellectual property while weaselling her way into things like reporting from New York Fashion Week and interviewing Molly Ringwald. She is now a freelance reporter in New York covering all of those topics and more for publications including Fashionista and The Wall Street Journal. Don’t follow her on Instagram if you’ll tire of pictures of Central Park, her chihuahua, or her 3 month old son, Reed. She tweets about law, lifestyle and everything in betweenhere._

**Mehdi Raza Hasan**[[a]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mehdi_Hasan#cite_note-1) (born 10 July 1979) is a British-American broadcaster, journalist, progressive political commentator, and founder of the media company Zeteo. He presented _The Mehdi Hasan Show_ on Peacock from October 2020 and on MSNBC from February 2021 until the show's cancellation in November 2023.

A graduate of Christ Church, Oxford, Hasan began his television career as a researcher and then producer on ITV's Jonathan Dimbleby programme. Following a stint on the BBC's _The Politics Show_, he became deputy executive producer on Sky's breakfast show _Sunrise_ before moving to Channel 4 as their editor of news and current affairs. In 2009, he was appointed senior editor for politics at the _New Statesman_. In 2012, he became a presenter on Al Jazeera English, and in 2015, he moved to Washington, D.C., to work full-time for Al Jazeera on _UpFront_ and host the _Deconstructed_ podcast produced by the online publication _The Intercept_ from 2018 to 2020.
Hasan is the author of _Win Every Argument_ and the co-author of a biography of former Labour Party leader Ed Miliband. He was formerly the political editor of the UK edition of _The Huffington Post_ and the presenter of the Al Jazeera English shows _The Café_, _Head to Head_, and _UpFront_. After departing MSNBC, Hasan joined _The Guardian_ as a columnist and created the digital media company Zeteo in February 2024, and returned as host of _Head to Head_ in June that year.

## Early life and education
Hasan was born on 10 July 1979[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mehdi_Hasan#cite_note-2)[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mehdi_Hasan#cite_note-3) in Swindon, Wiltshire, in South West England to Shia Muslim parents from Hyderabad in Telangana, Southern India.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mehdi_Hasan#cite_note-4)[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mehdi_Hasan#cite_note-tweet1-5)[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mehdi_Hasan#cite_note-6) His mother is a doctor and his father, an engineer. Hasan grew up in Harrow, an area of outer North West London.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mehdi_Hasan#cite_note-7)[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mehdi_Hasan#cite_note-:2-8)
Hasan was privately educated at [Merchant Taylors' School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Merchant_Taylors'_School,_Northwood "Merchant Taylors' School, Northwood"), an independent day school for boys at Sandy Lodge, in the Three Rivers District of Hertfordshire, near Northwood in North West London.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mehdi_Hasan#cite_note-mts-9) Hasan and British actor and rapper Riz Ahmed were classmates.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mehdi_Hasan#cite_note-:3-10) Hasan subsequently went up to Christ Church, University of Oxford, graduating in 2000 with a Bachelor of Arts (BA) degree in philosophy, politics and economics (PPE).[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mehdi_Hasan#cite_note-mts-9)

## Career
### 2009–2011: Early beginnings
Hasan worked as a researcher and then producer on ITV's _Jonathan Dimbleby_ programme,[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mehdi_Hasan#cite_note-telqt-11) with a brief period in between on BBC One's _The Politics Show_.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mehdi_Hasan#cite_note-telqt-11) Following this, he became deputy executive producer on Sky's breakfast show _Sunrise_,[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mehdi_Hasan#cite_note-telqt-11) before moving to Channel 4 as their editor of news and current affairs.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mehdi_Hasan#cite_note-pg-12) He was appointed senior editor for politics at the _New Statesman_ in late spring of 2009,[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mehdi_Hasan#cite_note-13) where he stayed until May 2012, then becoming political director of _The Huffington Post_ website.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mehdi_Hasan#cite_note-pg-12)[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mehdi_Hasan#cite_note-14)

## Career
### 2012–2020: _Al Jazeera_ and _The Intercept_
Hasan and Martin Kettle at a Labour Party conference in 2012
Hasan became a presenter on Al Jazeera's English news channel in May 2012.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mehdi_Hasan#cite_note-15) Hasan has appeared (six times) on the BBC's _Question Time_ programme,[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mehdi_Hasan#cite_note-16) and the Sunday morning programmes _The Big Questions_ and _Sunday Morning Live_.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mehdi_Hasan#cite_note-17)[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mehdi_Hasan#cite_note-18) On _Question Time_ in October 2013, Hasan called the _Daily Mail_ "immigrant-bashing, woman-hating, Muslim-smearing, NHS-undermining, [and] gay-baiting". The newspaper responded by printing an e-mail he had sent them in 2010, in which he asked for a column and praised several of their viewpoints. Hasan said the "sycophantic" letter was his writing but criticised the newspaper's decision to publish it.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mehdi_Hasan#cite_note-19)[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mehdi_Hasan#cite_note-20)
